extraction.body: Only tech companies are seeing growth from the AI boom, Apollo Global Management says. Apollo says that though some big companies are spending big on AI, they may soon pull back. Corporate America is starting to see AI spending not as a source of growth, but as a cost center. One of the world's largest investment firms says that only tech companies are getting a share of the AI pie . In an economic analysis published on Saturday, Apollo Global Management said that while the Magnificent Seven — a group of established tech companies that includes Nvidia and Meta — are seeing revenue growth during the AI boom, this growth isn't being shared by other industries. "Mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Torsten Slok, a partner and chief economist at Apollo, said in the report. "The technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech." In a series of graphs, Slok measured three main metrics that have boomed for tech companies but not for regular companies: revenue per worker, profit margins, and productivity growth. Since 2022, revenue per employee figures have skyrocketed for tech companies — rising from $550,000 to nearly $800,000 today. Meanwhile, that figure hasn't changed much for everyone else in the S&P 500, lingering around $550,000 for the last seven years. Similarly, while profit margins soared among tech companies since 2022, they've stagnated at about 10% for everyone else. And across the economy, AI hasn't yet dramatically increased productivity growth as some AI optimists have predicted. Apollo's research portends a dark shadow over a US economy throwing massive amounts of dough toward AI tools and companies, whose leaders have promised that an " age of abundance ," where people won't have to work as much, will soon be upon us. "The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins," Slok said. "That may be harder than it sounds," he added. If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

passages: “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok said.

Apollo’s Torsten Slok focuses on what he calls the S&P 493 — the S&P 500, minus Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla — finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat, with no evidence that AI is improving productivity.

AI hasn’t benefited the bottom line of any big corporations outside the tech industry, according to a note recently published by the chief economist at Apollo Global Management (the private equity giant that used to own TechCrunch).

Apollo’s Torsten Slok focuses on what he calls the S&P 493 — the S&P 500, minus Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla — finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat, with no evidence that AI is improving productivity. “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok said. Is this simply a matter of non-tech companies lagging behind the tech giants? Slok sounded skeptical, arguing that it will be tough for corporate America to “turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins.” “AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment,” he wrote, later adding, “AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.” Recent studies have also found that AI has yet to deliver significant productivity gains .

Torsten Slok's October 24 note found flat margins and revenue per worker across the S&P 493, even as Microsoft guides to $190 billion in 2026 AI capex and Meta plans up to $135 billion. Seven companies are carrying an AI boom that, by one economist's math, has yet to show up anywhere else in corporate America. That gap is now the central argument of the AI bubble skeptics. Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, published a note on October 24 making a specific, checkable claim: revenue per worker and profit margins have climbed for the Magnificent Seven since the AI spending wave began, and have stayed essentially flat for the other 493 companies in the S&P 500. Slok's own phrase for it, reported by Bloomberg, was that AI has delivered "zero payoff" to that broader group. Companies outside the Mag 7 are mentioning AI constantly on earnings calls, he found, but the mentions aren't translating into the numbers that are supposed to follow: faster revenue growth, fatter margins, or real cost savings. Slok's framing, also picked up by Fortune, is that mainstream corporate America is starting to treat AI token spending less like an investment and more like a cost center weighing on margins. That's a blunt reversal of the pitch every enterprise AI vendor has been selling for two years. If the companies buying the tools can't point to the return, the sales pitch has a hole in it. Here's why the distinction between the Mag 7 and the other 493 matters so much right now. Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet, Amazon and Nvidia are major sellers of AI chips, cloud capacity and related infrastructure, while all seven companies are investing heavily in AI. Microsoft reported $41 billion in capital spending in its latest quarter, up 70% from a year earlier, and said an accounting change would put its calendar-year 2026 guidance at roughly $175 billion while leaving the underlying investment plan unchanged. Meta has raised its 2026 capex guidance to $135 billion to $145 billion. Consensus estimates cited by Goldman Sachs put total 2026 capital spending by U.S. hyperscalers at about $800 billion, although not all of that spending is exclusively for AI. That's the spending side. Slok's aggregate charts show no comparable improvement in revenue per worker or profit margins among the other 493 companies. The comparison does not isolate AI's effect at individual companies or establish that AI caused the gap, but it shows that broad financial gains have yet to appear in those measures. CoreWeave's five-year CDS spread hit a record 1,194.5 basis points on October 15, implying roughly a 63% default probability, while Oracle's climbed near 300 basis points amid a $466 billion AI debt binge. - how AI company debt default risk is priced - CoreWeave credit default swap spread hits record high Slok's note landed less than two weeks after a sharper, faster scare in the market that funds the AI buildout. In mid-October, a chart about CoreWeave's debt load went viral on X after venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya flagged that the yield on $1.25 billion of the company's bonds due in 2032 had briefly touched 15%. CoreWeave, which is backed by Nvidia and had about $35 billion in debt plus roughly $16 billion in debt-like lease liabilities at the end of June, became a focal point for worries about AI financing. Its shares fell more than 15% on October 14, while yields on its unsecured bonds subsequently remained near 15%, as Oracle and several other AI infrastructure stocks also sold off. The CoreWeave scare was about leverage: a company borrowing heavily against future AI income it hasn't earned yet. Slok's note is a different and arguably more fundamental worry, about whether the income shows up at all once you look past the handful of companies both building and buying the infrastructure. Put those two stories next to each other and the AI trade starts to look like it's being carried by a very small number of balance sheets, both on the supply side and the demand side. Frankly, this is the number every founder selling an "AI productivity" tool into the enterprise should sit with. If S&P 500 companies with finance teams, procurement departments and CFOs under pressure to show ROI can't produce measurable gains from AI spending yet, that's a harder sell for a startup asking a mid-market customer to trust the same promise on a much smaller budget and a much shorter sales cycle. It doesn't mean the tools don't work. It means the case for them still runs on a story about the future, not a number from the last quarter. The second chart, "No signs of profit margins going up outside the tech sector," goes back further, to the first quarter of 2015.

Many of the AI features built into ad platforms - automated bidding, generated creative, agentic AI tools that run campaigns - are sold to these buyers on the promise of efficiency.

Rising Magnificent 7 margins could reflect AI-driven sales of cloud capacity, chips and advertising, but they also reflect cost cutting, layoffs, pricing power and cyclical factors that predate the current wave of generative AI.
The implication is that a large share of measured AI demand comes from companies whose spending depends on fresh capital rather than on operating profits.
The fourth and fifth charts carry that argument with spending data from Ramp, the corporate card and expense management company, which publishes the Ramp AI Index based on business transaction data.
The fourth chart, titled "AI spending is extremely concentrated in a small number of firms," is a table credited to Ara Kharazian, chief economist at Ramp, and Apollo's chief economist.

This matters because the huge sums being poured into AI chips, data centres and models only make sense if the thousands of companies buying AI eventually earn more from it.
For now, the data shows the gains staying with the biggest tech firms, while spending on AI services sits with a small group of mostly venture-backed companies.
Ray Dalio said earlier this month that his bubble indicator puts AI level with 1929 and 2000 .

Analyst Ed Zitron argued in August, citing UBS estimates, that OpenAI and Anthropic could make up more than 48% of Google Cloud revenue in 2027 - a concentration risk that echoes the Ramp data in Slok's note.

extraction.body: Top 10% of firms account for 99.5% of AI inference spend in Ramp data cited by Apollo. Can the rest of corporate America turn cheap tokens into higher margins? Artificial intelligence has delivered no measurable financial return to US companies outside the technology sector, according to Torsten Slok, partner and chief economist at Apollo Global Management, in a Daily Spark note published on October 24, 2026. The note, titled No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector , sets five charts side by side: revenue per worker, profit margins, productivity growth, the concentration of AI spending and the financial backing of the heaviest AI buyers. Its conclusion is blunt. "Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech," Slok wrote. A top economist at the investment firm Apollo looked at whether ordinary big US companies, not the tech giants, are making more money because of AI, and found no sign that they are. This matters because the huge sums being poured into AI chips, data centres and models only make sense if the thousands of companies buying AI eventually earn more from it. For now, the data shows the gains staying with the biggest tech firms, while spending on AI services sits with a small group of mostly venture-backed companies. The note's central device is a division of the S&P 500 into two unequal parts. The "Mag 7" - the seven largest US technology companies, usually counted as Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla - sit on one side. The remaining 493 constituents, which Slok calls the "S&P 493," sit on the other. Apollo's note does not list the seven names; the grouping is the conventional one used across financial markets. "Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493," Slok wrote. "Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493." The first chart, titled "Revenue per worker moving up for tech but not for the rest of the economy," tracks inflation-adjusted revenue per employee, in thousands of dollars at 2019 fourth-quarter prices, from the first quarter of 2019. On PPC Land's reading of the chart, the Magnificent 7 started the period at roughly $695,000 per employee, fell to a trough of about $565,000 around the turn of 2022 and 2023, and then climbed steadily to roughly $780,000 in the most recent quarter shown, with the sharpest jump at the very end of the series. The S&P 493 line moves within a much narrower band: about $495,000 in early 2019, a low near $465,000 in 2021, a peak around $548,000 in late 2022, and roughly $527,000 in the latest reading. Apollo credits Bloomberg, Macrobond and its own chief economist's office for the data. The second chart, "No signs of profit margins going up outside the tech sector," goes back further, to the first quarter of 2015. Reading from Apollo's chart, the Magnificent 7 profit margin rose from around 11% in 2015 to about 22% in early 2022, dropped to roughly 14% in 2023, and has since risen to close to 30%. The S&P 493 margin stood at about 8.5% in 2015, dipped to around 6.5% during the pandemic, peaked near 11.7% in early 2022, and has hovered between 9% and 10% since 2023. These figures are approximations taken from the plotted lines; Apollo did not publish the underlying values in the note. The shape matters as much as the level. For the largest technology companies, both revenue per worker and margins have accelerated in the period that coincides with heavy AI investment. For the rest of the index, the lines are close to flat over the same years. The third chart widens the lens from corporate accounts to the whole economy. Titled "No signs of AI boosting productivity growth," it plots two measures of year-over-year productivity growth from January 1985: labour output per hour from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, and total factor productivity, or TFP. The TFP series is the utilisation-adjusted measure maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (Fernald, 2014), which corrects for cyclical swings in how intensively capital and labour are used. The note goes further than describing flat lines. It makes a claim about corporate behaviour. "With no impact on the bottom line, mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Slok wrote. Token spending refers to the fees companies pay to AI providers for processing text and data, measured in tokens . The note does not quantify the pullback it describes, and it does not cite a survey for the shift in attitude. Other recent data points in the same direction. A KPMG survey of 2,145 senior leaders found that 49% had scaled back, narrowed, delayed or paused AI agent rollouts after costs began to outweigh value, while only 7% reported established return on investment. An August TransUnion study found that 53% of enterprise marketers reported meaningful ROI from AI, with most gains so far coming from time savings rather than revenue. Slok also draws a line between who buys AI and who does not. "VC-backed companies are spending more and more on tokens, but mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it," he wrote. "As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited." The fourth and fifth charts carry that argument with spending data from Ramp, the corporate card and expense management company, which publishes the Ramp AI Index based on business transaction data. The fourth chart, titled "AI spending is extremely concentrated in a small number of firms," is a table credited to Ara Kharazian, chief economist at Ramp, and Apollo's chief economist. It shows the share of spending in each category that comes from the top 10% of firms versus the bottom 90%. The note does not explain how the top 10% is defined - whether by total spend, category spend or company size - or what period the table covers. The most AI-specific categories are the most concentrated. Spending on model serving and inference cost - the computing bill for running AI models once they are trained - is almost entirely in the hands of the top tenth of firms, at 99.5%. Neoclouds, the specialist GPU cloud providers that rent computing capacity outside the large hyperscaler platforms, draw 99% of their spend from the same group. Direct payments to OpenAI and Anthropic, the two leading model developers, are 95.6% concentrated. Yet concentration is not unique to AI. Paid advertising, at 91.9%, is about as concentrated as conventional software-as-a-service spending, at 91.8%. Artificial intelligence has delivered no measurable financial return to US companies outside the technology sector, according to Torsten Slok, partner and chief economist at Apollo Global Management, in a Daily Spark note published on October 24, 2026. The note, titled No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector , sets five charts side by side: revenue per worker, profit margins, productivity growth, the concentration of AI spending and the financial backing of the heaviest AI buyers. Its conclusion is blunt. "Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech," Slok wrote.

A top economist at the investment firm Apollo looked at whether ordinary big US companies, not the tech giants, are making more money because of AI, and found no sign that they are. This matters because the huge sums being poured into AI chips, data centres and models only make sense if the thousands of companies buying AI eventually earn more from it. For now, the data shows the gains staying with the biggest tech firms, while spending on AI services sits with a small group of mostly venture-backed companies.

The note's central device is a division of the S&P 500 into two unequal parts. The "Mag 7" - the seven largest US technology companies, usually counted as Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla - sit on one side. The remaining 493 constituents, which Slok calls the "S&P 493," sit on the other. Apollo's note does not list the seven names; the grouping is the conventional one used across financial markets.
"Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493," Slok wrote. "Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493."

The first chart, titled "Revenue per worker moving up for tech but not for the rest of the economy," tracks inflation-adjusted revenue per employee, in thousands of dollars at 2019 fourth-quarter prices, from the first quarter of 2019. On PPC Land's reading of the chart, the Magnificent 7 started the period at roughly $695,000 per employee, fell to a trough of about $565,000 around the turn of 2022 and 2023, and then climbed steadily to roughly $780,000 in the most recent quarter shown, with the sharpest jump at the very end of the series. The S&P 493 line moves within a much narrower band: about $495,000 in early 2019, a low near $465,000 in 2021, a peak around $548,000 in late 2022, and roughly $527,000 in the latest reading. Apollo credits Bloomberg, Macrobond and its own chief economist's office for the data.

The second chart, "No signs of profit margins going up outside the tech sector," goes back further, to the first quarter of 2015. Reading from Apollo's chart, the Magnificent 7 profit margin rose from around 11% in 2015 to about 22% in early 2022, dropped to roughly 14% in 2023, and has since risen to close to 30%. The S&P 493 margin stood at about 8.5% in 2015, dipped to around 6.5% during the pandemic, peaked near 11.7% in early 2022, and has hovered between 9% and 10% since 2023. These figures are approximations taken from the plotted lines; Apollo did not publish the underlying values in the note.

The shape matters as much as the level. For the largest technology companies, both revenue per worker and margins have accelerated in the period that coincides with heavy AI investment. For the rest of the index, the lines are close to flat over the same years.

The third chart widens the lens from corporate accounts to the whole economy. Titled "No signs of AI boosting productivity growth," it plots two measures of year-over-year productivity growth from January 1985: labour output per hour from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, and total factor productivity, or TFP. The TFP series is the utilisation-adjusted measure maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (Fernald, 2014), which corrects for cyclical swings in how intensively capital and labour are used.

The note goes further than describing flat lines. It makes a claim about corporate behaviour. "With no impact on the bottom line, mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Slok wrote.

Token spending refers to the fees companies pay to AI providers for processing text and data, measured in tokens . The note does not quantify the pullback it describes, and it does not cite a survey for the shift in attitude. Other recent data points in the same direction. A KPMG survey of 2,145 senior leaders found that 49% had scaled back, narrowed, delayed or paused AI agent rollouts after costs began to outweigh value, while only 7% reported established return on investment. An August TransUnion study found that 53% of enterprise marketers reported meaningful ROI from AI, with most gains so far coming from time savings rather than revenue.

Slok also draws a line between who buys AI and who does not. "VC-backed companies are spending more and more on tokens, but mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it," he wrote. "As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited."

The fourth chart, titled "AI spending is extremely concentrated in a small number of firms," is a table credited to Ara Kharazian, chief economist at Ramp, and Apollo's chief economist. It shows the share of spending in each category that comes from the top 10% of firms versus the bottom 90%. The note does not explain how the top 10% is defined - whether by total spend, category spend or company size - or what period the table covers.

The most AI-specific categories are the most concentrated. Spending on model serving and inference cost - the computing bill for running AI models once they are trained - is almost entirely in the hands of the top tenth of firms, at 99.5%. Neoclouds, the specialist GPU cloud providers that rent computing capacity outside the large hyperscaler platforms, draw 99% of their spend from the same group. Direct payments to OpenAI and Anthropic, the two leading model developers, are 95.6% concentrated.

On June 30, 2026, he argued in a note titled "AI: The ROI Runway Could Be Long Outside the Tech Sector" that sectors such as health care, banking and energy face longer timelines to productivity gains than software companies, and that AI company valuations depend on margins eventually rising in the S&P 493. On August 9, 2026, in "The Buyers of AI Are Still Waiting for the Payoff" , he broke S&P 493 margins down by sector and argued that the capital spending boom was showing up in the margins of AI sellers, not buyers. The advertisers on the other side of those platforms are, for the most part, S&P 493 companies and smaller businesses. Whether that efficiency reaches their own profit and loss accounts is the question Apollo's charts say has not yet been answered.

extraction.body: Only tech companies are seeing growth from the AI boom, Apollo Global Management says. Apollo says that though some big companies are spending big on AI, they may soon pull back. Corporate America is starting to see AI spending not as a source of growth, but as a cost center. One of the world's largest investment firms says that only tech companies are getting a share of the AI pie . In an economic analysis published on Saturday, Apollo Global Management said that while the Magnificent Seven — a group of established tech companies that includes Nvidia and Meta — are seeing revenue growth during the AI boom, this growth isn't being shared by other industries. "Mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Torsten Slok, a partner and chief economist at Apollo, said in the report. "The technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech." In a series of graphs, Slok measured three main metrics that have boomed for tech companies but not for regular companies: revenue per worker, profit margins, and productivity growth. Since 2022, revenue per employee figures have skyrocketed for tech companies — rising from $550,000 to nearly $800,000 today. Meanwhile, that figure hasn't changed much for everyone else in the S&P 500, lingering around $550,000 for the last seven years. Similarly, while profit margins soared among tech companies since 2022, they've stagnated at about 10% for everyone else. And across the economy, AI hasn't yet dramatically increased productivity growth as some AI optimists have predicted. Apollo's research portends a dark shadow over a US economy throwing massive amounts of dough toward AI tools and companies, whose leaders have promised that an " age of abundance ," where people won't have to work as much, will soon be upon us. "The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins," Slok said. "That may be harder than it sounds," he added. If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

Torsten Slok's October 24 note found flat margins and revenue per worker across the S&P 493, even as Microsoft guides to $190 billion in 2026 AI capex and Meta plans up to $135 billion. Seven companies are carrying an AI boom that, by one economist's math, has yet to show up anywhere else in corporate America. That gap is now the central argument of the AI bubble skeptics. Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, published a note on October 24 making a specific, checkable claim: revenue per worker and profit margins have climbed for the Magnificent Seven since the AI spending wave began, and have stayed essentially flat for the other 493 companies in the S&P 500. Slok's own phrase for it, reported by Bloomberg, was that AI has delivered "zero payoff" to that broader group. Companies outside the Mag 7 are mentioning AI constantly on earnings calls, he found, but the mentions aren't translating into the numbers that are supposed to follow: faster revenue growth, fatter margins, or real cost savings. Slok's framing, also picked up by Fortune, is that mainstream corporate America is starting to treat AI token spending less like an investment and more like a cost center weighing on margins. That's a blunt reversal of the pitch every enterprise AI vendor has been selling for two years. If the companies buying the tools can't point to the return, the sales pitch has a hole in it. Here's why the distinction between the Mag 7 and the other 493 matters so much right now. Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet, Amazon and Nvidia are major sellers of AI chips, cloud capacity and related infrastructure, while all seven companies are investing heavily in AI. Microsoft reported $41 billion in capital spending in its latest quarter, up 70% from a year earlier, and said an accounting change would put its calendar-year 2026 guidance at roughly $175 billion while leaving the underlying investment plan unchanged. Meta has raised its 2026 capex guidance to $135 billion to $145 billion. Consensus estimates cited by Goldman Sachs put total 2026 capital spending by U.S. hyperscalers at about $800 billion, although not all of that spending is exclusively for AI. That's the spending side. Slok's aggregate charts show no comparable improvement in revenue per worker or profit margins among the other 493 companies. The comparison does not isolate AI's effect at individual companies or establish that AI caused the gap, but it shows that broad financial gains have yet to appear in those measures. CoreWeave's five-year CDS spread hit a record 1,194.5 basis points on October 15, implying roughly a 63% default probability, while Oracle's climbed near 300 basis points amid a $466 billion AI debt binge. - how AI company debt default risk is priced - CoreWeave credit default swap spread hits record high Slok's note landed less than two weeks after a sharper, faster scare in the market that funds the AI buildout. In mid-October, a chart about CoreWeave's debt load went viral on X after venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya flagged that the yield on $1.25 billion of the company's bonds due in 2032 had briefly touched 15%. CoreWeave, which is backed by Nvidia and had about $35 billion in debt plus roughly $16 billion in debt-like lease liabilities at the end of June, became a focal point for worries about AI financing. Its shares fell more than 15% on October 14, while yields on its unsecured bonds subsequently remained near 15%, as Oracle and several other AI infrastructure stocks also sold off. The CoreWeave scare was about leverage: a company borrowing heavily against future AI income it hasn't earned yet. Slok's note is a different and arguably more fundamental worry, about whether the income shows up at all once you look past the handful of companies both building and buying the infrastructure. Put those two stories next to each other and the AI trade starts to look like it's being carried by a very small number of balance sheets, both on the supply side and the demand side. Frankly, this is the number every founder selling an "AI productivity" tool into the enterprise should sit with. If S&P 500 companies with finance teams, procurement departments and CFOs under pressure to show ROI can't produce measurable gains from AI spending yet, that's a harder sell for a startup asking a mid-market customer to trust the same promise on a much smaller budget and a much shorter sales cycle. It doesn't mean the tools don't work. It means the case for them still runs on a story about the future, not a number from the last quarter. It doesn't mean the tools don't work. It means the case for them still runs on a story about the future, not a number from the last quarter.

extraction.body: Top 10% of firms account for 99.5% of AI inference spend in Ramp data cited by Apollo. Can the rest of corporate America turn cheap tokens into higher margins? Artificial intelligence has delivered no measurable financial return to US companies outside the technology sector, according to Torsten Slok, partner and chief economist at Apollo Global Management, in a Daily Spark note published on October 24, 2026. The note, titled No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector , sets five charts side by side: revenue per worker, profit margins, productivity growth, the concentration of AI spending and the financial backing of the heaviest AI buyers. Its conclusion is blunt. "Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech," Slok wrote. A top economist at the investment firm Apollo looked at whether ordinary big US companies, not the tech giants, are making more money because of AI, and found no sign that they are. This matters because the huge sums being poured into AI chips, data centres and models only make sense if the thousands of companies buying AI eventually earn more from it. For now, the data shows the gains staying with the biggest tech firms, while spending on AI services sits with a small group of mostly venture-backed companies. The note's central device is a division of the S&P 500 into two unequal parts. The "Mag 7" - the seven largest US technology companies, usually counted as Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla - sit on one side. The remaining 493 constituents, which Slok calls the "S&P 493," sit on the other. Apollo's note does not list the seven names; the grouping is the conventional one used across financial markets. "Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493," Slok wrote. "Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493." The first chart, titled "Revenue per worker moving up for tech but not for the rest of the economy," tracks inflation-adjusted revenue per employee, in thousands of dollars at 2019 fourth-quarter prices, from the first quarter of 2019. On PPC Land's reading of the chart, the Magnificent 7 started the period at roughly $695,000 per employee, fell to a trough of about $565,000 around the turn of 2022 and 2023, and then climbed steadily to roughly $780,000 in the most recent quarter shown, with the sharpest jump at the very end of the series. The S&P 493 line moves within a much narrower band: about $495,000 in early 2019, a low near $465,000 in 2021, a peak around $548,000 in late 2022, and roughly $527,000 in the latest reading. Apollo credits Bloomberg, Macrobond and its own chief economist's office for the data. The second chart, "No signs of profit margins going up outside the tech sector," goes back further, to the first quarter of 2015. Reading from Apollo's chart, the Magnificent 7 profit margin rose from around 11% in 2015 to about 22% in early 2022, dropped to roughly 14% in 2023, and has since risen to close to 30%. The S&P 493 margin stood at about 8.5% in 2015, dipped to around 6.5% during the pandemic, peaked near 11.7% in early 2022, and has hovered between 9% and 10% since 2023. These figures are approximations taken from the plotted lines; Apollo did not publish the underlying values in the note. The shape matters as much as the level. For the largest technology companies, both revenue per worker and margins have accelerated in the period that coincides with heavy AI investment. For the rest of the index, the lines are close to flat over the same years. The third chart widens the lens from corporate accounts to the whole economy. Titled "No signs of AI boosting productivity growth," it plots two measures of year-over-year productivity growth from January 1985: labour output per hour from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, and total factor productivity, or TFP. The TFP series is the utilisation-adjusted measure maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (Fernald, 2014), which corrects for cyclical swings in how intensively capital and labour are used. The note goes further than describing flat lines. It makes a claim about corporate behaviour. "With no impact on the bottom line, mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Slok wrote. Token spending refers to the fees companies pay to AI providers for processing text and data, measured in tokens . The note does not quantify the pullback it describes, and it does not cite a survey for the shift in attitude. Other recent data points in the same direction. A KPMG survey of 2,145 senior leaders found that 49% had scaled back, narrowed, delayed or paused AI agent rollouts after costs began to outweigh value, while only 7% reported established return on investment. An August TransUnion study found that 53% of enterprise marketers reported meaningful ROI from AI, with most gains so far coming from time savings rather than revenue. Slok also draws a line between who buys AI and who does not. "VC-backed companies are spending more and more on tokens, but mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it," he wrote. "As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited." The fourth and fifth charts carry that argument with spending data from Ramp, the corporate card and expense management company, which publishes the Ramp AI Index based on business transaction data. The fourth chart, titled "AI spending is extremely concentrated in a small number of firms," is a table credited to Ara Kharazian, chief economist at Ramp, and Apollo's chief economist. It shows the share of spending in each category that comes from the top 10% of firms versus the bottom 90%. The note does not explain how the top 10% is defined - whether by total spend, category spend or company size - or what period the table covers. The most AI-specific categories are the most concentrated. Spending on model serving and inference cost - the computing bill for running AI models once they are trained - is almost entirely in the hands of the top tenth of firms, at 99.5%. Neoclouds, the specialist GPU cloud providers that rent computing capacity outside the large hyperscaler platforms, draw 99% of their spend from the same group. Direct payments to OpenAI and Anthropic, the two leading model developers, are 95.6% concentrated. Yet concentration is not unique to AI. Paid advertising, at 91.9%, is about as concentrated as conventional software-as-a-service spending, at 91.8%. CRM software is the least concentrated category in the table, with the bottom 90% of firms accounting for 15.8% of spend. The comparison suggests that the top tenth of firms dominates business spending in general, and AI spending more so. For the advertising industry, the paid ads row is a reminder that a small share of companies already accounts for most ad budgets in Ramp's dataset. If AI spending follows the same pattern but more steeply, the companies best placed to deploy AI in marketing are, for now, the same ones that already carry the largest media budgets. The fifth chart is titled "Circularity in AI shows up in token spending too." Based on the Ramp AI Index, it splits businesses by AI spend intensity and shows whether they are backed by venture capital. Among the top 1% of AI spenders, 80.4% are VC-backed and 19.6% are not. Among median spenders, the proportions flip: 13.1% are VC-backed and 86.9% are not. The chart's title links that finding to a wider debate about circular financing in the AI industry, in which investors fund AI start-ups that then spend much of that money on cloud computing and model access from companies tied to the same investors. Slok's note does not spell out the mechanism. Its data shows only that the heaviest token buyers are overwhelmingly funded by venture capital, while the typical business buying AI is not. The implication is that a large share of measured AI demand comes from companies whose spending depends on fresh capital rather than on operating profits. That is not the same as demand from mainstream companies paying for AI out of improved margins - the outcome the S&P 493 charts say has not yet arrived. Slok frames the open question as whether falling prices change the picture. "The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins," he wrote. "That may be harder than it sounds." His reasoning is qualitative. "AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment," Slok wrote. "Judgment depends on context, and the answer varies with which human or which model you ask." He added that "AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins." The note closes on a single sentence that summarises the argument: "The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector." The charts show correlation in time, not cause. Rising Magnificent 7 margins could reflect AI-driven sales of cloud capacity, chips and advertising, but they also reflect cost cutting, layoffs, pricing power and cyclical factors that predate the current wave of generative AI. The flat S&P 493 lines do not prove AI has no effect at company level; gains in some firms or sectors could be offset by losses elsewhere, or could take longer to show up in aggregate figures. The note's claim that mainstream companies are "pulling back" on token spending is not backed by a specific data series in the note itself. The Ramp figures also come with limits. They reflect businesses that use Ramp's cards and expense software, not the economy as a whole, and they are not the same population as the S&P 493 in the first two charts. The note does not state the sample size, time period or definition of the top 10%. The October 24 note is the latest in a run of Daily Spark entries in which Slok has tracked the gap between AI investment and returns outside technology. On June 30, 2026, he argued in a note titled "AI: The ROI Runway Could Be Long Outside the Tech Sector" that sectors such as health care, banking and energy face longer timelines to productivity gains than software companies, and that AI company valuations depend on margins eventually rising in the S&P 493. On August 9, 2026, in "The Buyers of AI Are Still Waiting for the Payoff" , he broke S&P 493 margins down by sector and argued that the capital spending boom was showing up in the margins of AI sellers, not buyers. The October note adds the revenue-per-worker comparison, the productivity series and the Ramp spending data. The advertising market sits on both sides of Slok's divide. Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft are among the Magnificent 7 and earn much of their revenue from advertising, which in turn funds their AI infrastructure. Alphabet guided to $175 billion to $185 billion in 2026 capital expenditure when it reported fourth-quarter 2025 results in February. Microsoft said in April that its AI business had passed a $37 billion annual revenue run rate , up 123% year over year, with quarterly capital spending of $31.9 billion. Google said this month that Gemini 4 Argon processed almost 25 trillion tokens in its first 72 hours , and that the company remains capacity constrained. The advertisers on the other side of those platforms are, for the most part, S&P 493 companies and smaller businesses. When their margins are flat, marketing budgets come under the same scrutiny Slok describes for token spending. Many of the AI features built into ad platforms - automated bidding, generated creative, agentic AI tools that run campaigns - are sold to these buyers on the promise of efficiency. Whether that efficiency reaches their own profit and loss accounts is the question Apollo's charts say has not yet been answered. Measurement on the buyer side remains thin. A Basis survey published on October 19 found that only 6.5% of 184 organisations measured AI returns against defined benchmarks, even as 88.6% paid for premium AI tools. Survey-based studies tend to show more optimism than the aggregate data: Meta's YouGov survey of 3,983 Asia-Pacific small business owners found 76% reporting a productivity gain, though those were owners' own assessments rather than measured outcomes. Google's AI and Economy ATLAS report found AI usage in 68% of occupations but a median of 21% of tasks within those jobs. The broader market debate has sharpened too. Ray Dalio said earlier this month that his bubble indicator puts AI level with 1929 and 2000 . Analyst Ed Zitron argued in August, citing UBS estimates, that OpenAI and Anthropic could make up more than 48% of Google Cloud revenue in 2027 - a concentration risk that echoes the Ramp data in Slok's note. Apollo's chief economist adds a different kind of evidence to that debate: not valuations or financing, but the plain accounts of the companies that are supposed to be AI's customers. Who: Torsten Slok, partner and chief economist at Apollo Global Management, using data from Bloomberg, Macrobond, the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics and Ramp, including Ramp chief economist Ara Kharazian. What: A Daily Spark note arguing that AI has delivered "zero financial payoff" to US companies outside tech. Revenue per worker and profit margins have risen for the Magnificent 7 but stayed flat for the S&P 493, productivity growth shows no AI effect, the top 10% of firms account for 99.5% of model serving and inference spend in Ramp data, and 80.4% of the top 1% of AI spenders are venture-backed. When: Published October 24, 2026, following related Apollo notes on June 30 and August 9, 2026. Where: The United States, with the analysis centred on S&P 500 companies and Ramp's business spending data. Why: The returns on AI investment depend on mainstream companies turning AI into higher revenue and margins. Slok argues that this has not happened yet, and that while AI spending stays concentrated among a small group of mostly venture-backed firms, its effect on the wider economy will remain limited. For advertisers and the platforms that sell to them, the question is whether AI-driven efficiency will reach buyers' own profit and loss accounts. extraction.body: Co-ordinated protests have taken place across the country with a heavy security presence in most cities Thousands of people have marched in South Africa's main cities to demand that all undocumented migrants leave the country. Police officers - backed by private security guards - have been deployed because of fears that protests could turn violent. Anti-migrant groups had set Tuesday as the deadline for undocumented migrants to leave. Many foreigners have already fled to escape violence and intimidation. South African police say 25,000 have been repatriated so far. Most are from other African countries. However Police Minister Firoz Cachalia confirmed that the army was deployed "on a contingency basis" in parts of Johannesburg as well as Durban. Police also confirmed the arrest of three people in Hillbrow, a suburb in Johannesburg with a high migrant population, after two people were injured during protests. According to police, the trio "opened fire at protesters who were passing through the street" and the marchers retaliated by "torching the suspects' vehicle". Among the injured was a 17-year-old. Some protesters threw bricks, breaking the windows of some homes in Yeoville, another suburb where many African migrants live. Police said they had arrested five people for the alleged looting of a foreign-owned shop in Johannesburg's biggest township, Soweto. About 10 people were also arrested for looting in KwaZulu-Natal province, while a woman was arrested for assaulting a police officer and a man for "intimidation" following reports of a foreign national being beaten up, police said. Businesses in central Durban, the main city in the province, were also shut. Protesters handed over a memorandum listing their demands to government officials in Durban and Johannesburg. The leader of anti-migrant group March and March, Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, said they would protest every Thursday for the next six months to force the government to "get rid of" undocumented migrants who were still in South Africa. A demonstrator - who is part of another anti-migrant group, Operation Dudula - told the BBC they would "push the police" to arrest foreigners who are not legally in the country. President Cyril Ramaphosa met some of the protest leaders on the eve of Tuesday's marches to defuse tensions. Anti-migrant protesters march in South Africa "Some foreign nationals who live in South Africa are here lawfully," he reminded citizens in his weekly newsletter , external . "The right to protest and freedom of expression does not allow people to threaten or intimidate others, or to engage in acts of vandalism or violence," he wrote. There are more than three million documented foreign nationals in South Africa, according to official figures. The statistics do not record the many more migrants believed to be in the country without papers - a bone of contention for the protesters. Many African migrants moved to South Africa around the time white-minority rule ended in 1994, hoping for a better life. But with South Africa facing an unemployment rate of more than 30%, anti-migrant sentiments have risen. Nigeria flew out 269 of its citizens on the eve of the protests, bringing to around 600 the number evacuated so far to the West African nation. More evacuations are expected to take place in the coming days. Women in colourful sarongs sat on top of their belongings, waiting in line to board a bus home to Malawi. One man, Nelson Mbewe, said he had gone to South Africa in search of employment to support his family in Malawi. "But we've faced challenges - they're saying we should go back home because we do not have the right documents," he told the BBC. "It's their country, so what can we do? That's why we have accepted that we just have to [unwillingly] go back home." Hassan Phiri, a Malawian who is still waiting to be processed, had a message for the protesters: "All I want to say to South Africans is that we are all one. No matter what is happening, no matter what will happen, Africa must remain Africa. "Africa can't be Africa without South Africa... without Malawi, without anywhere," he told the BBC, adding: "So whatever will happen, we must love each other and stick together as Africa." "We have no money for transport, food and shelter as we attempt to proceed to Malawi. We request both the governments of Malawi and Mozambique to come to our aid," a Malawian man who had worked in South Africa for more than 20 years told local media. Anti-migrant marches were authorised in Durban, Johannesburg and other cities, with police saying traditional weapons would not be allowed. It was feared this would lead to tension between protesters and the police as many of the demonstrators are ethnic Zulus, who take their shields, whips and sticks when they go on marches. However, police have so far allowed them to carry the weapons, seizing only a machete at a march in Durban. sources.title: Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policing - The Guardian
passages: Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president.
More than 70,000 police were on the streets of French cities, with shops boarded up and many museums closed.
The government estimated that at least 400,000 people had marched across France.

A 21-year-old student from a Paris science faculty that is now blockaded by demonstrators said: “We feel in France that we are increasingly living in an authoritarian regime that is trying to stop our democratic right to protest in the street.”
The radical left presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who took part in the Paris rally, said Macron must “give in” and address France’s social malaise or face repeated protests.
“Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week,” Mélenchon said.

They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions.

The government has been facing a crisis since the start of high school demonstrations in mid-September, when children aged between 15 and 18 began protesting against staff shortages at their schools, leaking and crumbling buildings, and a lack of chairs in overcrowded classrooms.
In Orléans, thousands shouting anti-fascist slogans marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen’s far-right anti-immigration National Rally party.
But at times it really does feel like a war … This is the first time I’ve prepared so carefully for a peaceful march, wearing old clothes in case they are gassed or torn.”

extraction.body: Almost 1,000 arrested as police charge crowd in Paris and teargas used to stop protesters reaching other city centres Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president. The prosecutor’s office in the southern city of Nice said on Sunday that 59 people had been taken into police custody, including 11 suspected of belonging to extreme-right groups. They were alleged to have gathered with the intent of committing violence. Some were arrested in two vehicles with masks, gloves, gas sprays and truncheons, the prosecutor’s office said in a statement to public broadcaster FranceInfo. Local media in Nice had reported extreme-right groups coming to the city centre and targeting demonstrators on Saturday. In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates. They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions. The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”. But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city’s eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police. Riot police also charged a larger crowd of protesters at the end of the Paris march, using batons against them. Police fired teargas to prevent protesters in Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse from reaching city centres. In Marseille, some bin fires were lit amid clashes with police. At least two people were seriously injured, one in Clermont-Ferrand and another in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off. The government estimated that at least 400,000 people had marched across France. Trade unions estimated the number at double that. The interior ministry said there had been 1,314 arrests, 75 fires and 24 shops looted – less than last weekend. Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, said that at various street marches across France there were what he called “high-risk groups” who “broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence”. More than 70,000 police were on the streets of French cities, with shops boarded up and many museums closed. The government had feared a repeat of last Saturday, when, despite peaceful protests taking place, France saw one of the most violent days of unrest in years, with public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,700 people arrested in cities across the country. At Saturday’s protests, there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres. At the Paris march, Nadège, a 43-year-old communications worker, said she had been teargassed last weekend at a peaceful demonstration. “I’m out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now. We have to keep our rights alive … In France, it’s our legal right to protest in the street and I’m here to defend that.” A 21-year-old student from a Paris science faculty that is now blockaded by demonstrators said: “We feel in France that we are increasingly living in an authoritarian regime that is trying to stop our democratic right to protest in the street.” The radical left presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who took part in the Paris rally, said Macron must “give in” and address France’s social malaise or face repeated protests. “Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week,” Mélenchon said. The government has been facing a crisis since the start of high school demonstrations in mid-September, when children aged between 15 and 18 began protesting against staff shortages at their schools, leaking and crumbling buildings, and a lack of chairs in overcrowded classrooms. It grew into the biggest youth movement in years, with trade unions, teachers and parents joining. Police investigations are under way after some children and protesters were maimed and injured by explosive police weaponry. At Saturday’s march there were some people dressed in yellow vests who had taken part in the gilets jaunes anti-government protests of 2018 and 2019. Standing amid demonstrators, Jérôme Rodrigues, a key figure from the gilets jaunes protest, said: “Today the government is afraid; that is why they are pushing demonstrators to the edge of the city, away from places of power. It’s not police shields that will provide an answer to French people struggling and unable to make ends meet.” He said it was likely that demonstrations would continue. Pierre, 60, a retired banking consultant, said he was demonstrating in support of school students. “I have an eight-year-old granddaughter. I want her to have a brighter future than the sombre times we are facing today. There is a complete refusal by the government to listen to people’s demands.” Jesse, 40, a charity worker from the north of Paris, carrying a sign saying “Free Hugs”, said: “I’m so angry. I’m here to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions. I’m so proud of them, and we have to stand together.” She said: “I know I’m not going to war by coming out to demonstrate peacefully. But at times it really does feel like a war … This is the first time I’ve prepared so carefully for a peaceful march, wearing old clothes in case they are gassed or torn.” In Orléans, thousands shouting anti-fascist slogans marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen’s far-right anti-immigration National Rally party. Protesters criticised Le Pen, a frontrunner in next year’s presidential election, as well as Macron, who steps down from power next year. “Macron, resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd shouted.

At the Paris march, Nadège, a 43-year-old communications worker, said she had been teargassed last weekend at a peaceful demonstration. “I’m out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now. We have to keep our rights alive … In France, it’s our legal right to protest in the street and I’m here to defend that.”

A 21-year-old student from a Paris science faculty that is now blockaded by demonstrators said: “We feel in France that we are increasingly living in an authoritarian regime that is trying to stop our democratic right to protest in the street.”

The radical left presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who took part in the Paris rally, said Macron must “give in” and address France’s social malaise or face repeated protests. “Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week,” Mélenchon said.

The government has been facing a crisis since the start of high school demonstrations in mid-September, when children aged between 15 and 18 began protesting against staff shortages at their schools, leaking and crumbling buildings, and a lack of chairs in overcrowded classrooms. It grew into the biggest youth movement in years, with trade unions, teachers and parents joining. Police investigations are under way after some children and protesters were maimed and injured by explosive police weaponry.

At Saturday’s march there were some people dressed in yellow vests who had taken part in the gilets jaunes anti-government protests of 2018 and 2019. Standing amid demonstrators, Jérôme Rodrigues, a key figure from the gilets jaunes protest, said: “Today the government is afraid; that is why they are pushing demonstrators to the edge of the city, away from places of power. It’s not police shields that will provide an answer to French people struggling and unable to make ends meet.” He said it was likely that demonstrations would continue.

Pierre, 60, a retired banking consultant, said he was demonstrating in support of school students. “I have an eight-year-old granddaughter. I want her to have a brighter future than the sombre times we are facing today. There is a complete refusal by the government to listen to people’s demands.”

Jesse, 40, a charity worker from the north of Paris, carrying a sign saying “Free Hugs”, said: “I’m so angry. I’m here to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions. I’m so proud of them, and we have to stand together.”

She said: “I know I’m not going to war by coming out to demonstrate peacefully. But at times it really does feel like a war … This is the first time I’ve prepared so carefully for a peaceful march, wearing old clothes in case they are gassed or torn.”

In Orléans, thousands shouting anti-fascist slogans marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen’s far-right anti-immigration National Rally party. Protesters criticised Le Pen, a frontrunner in next year’s presidential election, as well as Macron, who steps down from power next year. “Macron, resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd shouted.

A record number of police officers patrolled the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, while St. Louis resumed its annual parade, canceled last year amid protests over Michael Brown's death. Here's a look at how Americans celebrated: --Spectators at the annual Macy's parade in New York noted a stepped-up police presence, with officers perched on buildings like Radio City Music Hall and watching from helicopters hovering overhead. “It's a little scary, but at least it's keeping us safe,” Kim Miller of Boston said of the heavy security. “We're having fun.” City officials said there were no known credible threats against New York following the deadly attacks eight days earlier in Paris and a video purportedly produced by the Islamic State group that contained footage of Times Square. Bratton said more than 2,500 officers would nevertheless be stationed along the parade route for the Thanksgiving festivities — the largest number of officers the department has ever assigned to the event. The parade, in its 89th year, included marching bands and floats along with Hello Kitty, Snoopy, SpongeBob SquarePants and other giant balloons. Pamela and Tom Popp of Ridgefield, N.J., said they've come to the parade every year for at least 20 years. “It's just a very special part of our holiday,” Pamela Popp said. “We're very proud of New York City and this wonderful tradition.” Her husband noted the right security. “I see the cops on top of Radio City,” Tom Popp said. Louis, a modest-sized crowd gathered on an unseasonably warm morning for the annual Thanksgiving Day parade that was canceled last year amid protests and widespread unrest resulting in multiple arrests over the death of Brown, an unarmed black 18-year-old and other police shootings. The 2014 parade was supposed to be held several days after a St. Louis County grand jury decided to not indict former Ferguson police Officer Darren Wilson, who is white, in Brown's death. --In Illinois, after two days of demonstrations following the release of a video that shows a white Chicago police officer shooting and killing black teenager Laquan McDonald in 2014, protest organizers said there were no marches planned for Thanksgiving Day. Instead, they said they were preparing for a march through the city's famed shopping district, the Magnificent Mile, on Friday. PARIS >> Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets of France today as a vastly reinforced security presence appeared to have averted a repeat of last weekend’s unrest, despite isolated clashes in several cities. About 110,000 people marched peacefully through the French capital, according to police numbers. Waving flags, they denounced the growing cost of living and rising inequality. “Down with the state, the police and the fascists,” the crowd chanted. At the end of the march, police fired tear gas and used water cannon to try to disperse small groups of hooded youths, but the violence was far less than last Saturday, when looters and vandals went on the rampage in Paris. Clashes also flared in Lyon, Bordeaux and Grenoble, while police fired volleys of tear gas at demonstrators in Clermont-Ferrand, Lille and Nice. In France’s second city, Marseille, youths dragged large metal sheets to block a street, set fire to rubbish bins, and hurled rocks and bottles at riot police, with the confrontations continuing as night fell. Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE! The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in nationwide protests, while unions claimed turnout was double that. Authorities deployed 70,000 police officers and gendarmes, 10,000 more than a week earlier, after conceding they had underestimated the scale of the unrest. “We have to be ultra, ultra responsive,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters, accusing far-left activists and criminal gangs of seeking to foment violence. Nunez told reporters that police had arrested 135 people nationwide by early afternoon, many following pre-emptive searches that he said had uncovered fireworks, ball bearings and other items that could be used as weapons. Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers boarding up storefronts, museums closing their doors and more than 20 metro stations shut. Business groups urged retailers to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend. “There are hardly any customers, so it’s not really worth staying open,” said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris. Several of the capital’s best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musee d’Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated. “Everything’s boarded up and we’re not quite sure where we should be,” said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from New Orleans, Lousiana. The nationwide unrest began with small student demonstrations in suburban Paris last month to denounce school conditions. After it spread into a broader protest against the state of the economy in France, it also prompted demonstrators to take to the streets in neighbouring countries. Today, Belgian police used tear gas and pepper spray as they clashed in Brussels with anti-government demonstrators, while protests took place in Italian cities for a second weekend. Leftist leaders in France denounced a government move to limit the number of authorized marches in many cities, as well as a last-minute decision to shift the Paris event to the southeastern fringes of the capital. Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who joined the Paris rally, hailed what he called a “magnificent mass display of collective discipline and self-restraint”. He predicted the protests would continue until President Emmanuel Macron, whose mandate expires next year, addressed the social malaise in France, one of the world’s richest nations but with a growing debt mountain that has alarmed investors. “Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door,” Melenchon told reporters. Many demonstrators have accused the government of overreacting, as soldiers were dispatched to patrol the Champs-Elysees, a grand boulevard lined with luxury shops and restaurants. “We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round,” said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student. “My friend and I almost didn’t come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it’s important not to let repression win,” she added. The first authorised march today passed off peacefully in Orleans, around 75 miles south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally, which is holding a party congress in the city. A shooting west of Paris on Friday heightened tensions. A gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl. “We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid,” said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon’s France Unbowed party. 500 Ala Moana Blvd. #2-200 Honolulu, HI 96813 (808) 529-4747

extraction.body: Co-ordinated protests have taken place across the country with a heavy security presence in most cities Thousands of people have marched in South Africa's main cities to demand that all undocumented migrants leave the country. Police officers - backed by private security guards - have been deployed because of fears that protests could turn violent. Anti-migrant groups had set Tuesday as the deadline for undocumented migrants to leave. Many foreigners have already fled to escape violence and intimidation. South African police say 25,000 have been repatriated so far. Most are from other African countries. However Police Minister Firoz Cachalia confirmed that the army was deployed "on a contingency basis" in parts of Johannesburg as well as Durban. Police also confirmed the arrest of three people in Hillbrow, a suburb in Johannesburg with a high migrant population, after two people were injured during protests. According to police, the trio "opened fire at protesters who were passing through the street" and the marchers retaliated by "torching the suspects' vehicle". Among the injured was a 17-year-old. Some protesters threw bricks, breaking the windows of some homes in Yeoville, another suburb where many African migrants live. Police said they had arrested five people for the alleged looting of a foreign-owned shop in Johannesburg's biggest township, Soweto. About 10 people were also arrested for looting in KwaZulu-Natal province, while a woman was arrested for assaulting a police officer and a man for "intimidation" following reports of a foreign national being beaten up, police said. Businesses in central Durban, the main city in the province, were also shut. Protesters handed over a memorandum listing their demands to government officials in Durban and Johannesburg. The leader of anti-migrant group March and March, Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, said they would protest every Thursday for the next six months to force the government to "get rid of" undocumented migrants who were still in South Africa. A demonstrator - who is part of another anti-migrant group, Operation Dudula - told the BBC they would "push the police" to arrest foreigners who are not legally in the country. President Cyril Ramaphosa met some of the protest leaders on the eve of Tuesday's marches to defuse tensions. Anti-migrant protesters march in South Africa "Some foreign nationals who live in South Africa are here lawfully," he reminded citizens in his weekly newsletter , external . "The right to protest and freedom of expression does not allow people to threaten or intimidate others, or to engage in acts of vandalism or violence," he wrote. There are more than three million documented foreign nationals in South Africa, according to official figures. The statistics do not record the many more migrants believed to be in the country without papers - a bone of contention for the protesters. Many African migrants moved to South Africa around the time white-minority rule ended in 1994, hoping for a better life. But with South Africa facing an unemployment rate of more than 30%, anti-migrant sentiments have risen. Nigeria flew out 269 of its citizens on the eve of the protests, bringing to around 600 the number evacuated so far to the West African nation. More evacuations are expected to take place in the coming days. Women in colourful sarongs sat on top of their belongings, waiting in line to board a bus home to Malawi. One man, Nelson Mbewe, said he had gone to South Africa in search of employment to support his family in Malawi. "But we've faced challenges - they're saying we should go back home because we do not have the right documents," he told the BBC. "It's their country, so what can we do? That's why we have accepted that we just have to [unwillingly] go back home." Hassan Phiri, a Malawian who is still waiting to be processed, had a message for the protesters: "All I want to say to South Africans is that we are all one. No matter what is happening, no matter what will happen, Africa must remain Africa. "Africa can't be Africa without South Africa... without Malawi, without anywhere," he told the BBC, adding: "So whatever will happen, we must love each other and stick together as Africa." "We have no money for transport, food and shelter as we attempt to proceed to Malawi. We request both the governments of Malawi and Mozambique to come to our aid," a Malawian man who had worked in South Africa for more than 20 years told local media. Anti-migrant marches were authorised in Durban, Johannesburg and other cities, with police saying traditional weapons would not be allowed. It was feared this would lead to tension between protesters and the police as many of the demonstrators are ethnic Zulus, who take their shields, whips and sticks when they go on marches. However, police have so far allowed them to carry the weapons, seizing only a machete at a march in Durban. extraction.body: Almost 1,000 arrested as police charge crowd in Paris and teargas used to stop protesters reaching other city centres Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president. The prosecutor’s office in the southern city of Nice said on Sunday that 59 people had been taken into police custody, including 11 suspected of belonging to extreme-right groups. They were alleged to have gathered with the intent of committing violence. Some were arrested in two vehicles with masks, gloves, gas sprays and truncheons, the prosecutor’s office said in a statement to public broadcaster FranceInfo. Local media in Nice had reported extreme-right groups coming to the city centre and targeting demonstrators on Saturday. In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates. They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions. The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”. But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city’s eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police. Riot police also charged a larger crowd of protesters at the end of the Paris march, using batons against them. Police fired teargas to prevent protesters in Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse from reaching city centres. In Marseille, some bin fires were lit amid clashes with police. extraction.body: Americans paused Thursday to celebrate their blessings despite terrorism fears and racial tensions over fatal police shootings across the country. A record number of police officers patrolled the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, while St. Louis resumed its annual parade, canceled last year amid protests over Michael Brown's death. Here's a look at how Americans celebrated: --Spectators at the annual Macy's parade in New York noted a stepped-up police presence, with officers perched on buildings like Radio City Music Hall and watching from helicopters hovering overhead. “It's a little scary, but at least it's keeping us safe,” Kim Miller of Boston said of the heavy security. “We're having fun.” City officials said there were no known credible threats against New York following the deadly attacks eight days earlier in Paris and a video purportedly produced by the Islamic State group that contained footage of Times Square. Bratton said more than 2,500 officers would nevertheless be stationed along the parade route for the Thanksgiving festivities — the largest number of officers the department has ever assigned to the event. The parade, in its 89th year, included marching bands and floats along with Hello Kitty, Snoopy, SpongeBob SquarePants and other giant balloons. Pamela and Tom Popp of Ridgefield, N.J., said they've come to the parade every year for at least 20 years. “It's just a very special part of our holiday,” Pamela Popp said. “We're very proud of New York City and this wonderful tradition.” Her husband noted the right security. “I see the cops on top of Radio City,” Tom Popp said. Louis, a modest-sized crowd gathered on an unseasonably warm morning for the annual Thanksgiving Day parade that was canceled last year amid protests and widespread unrest resulting in multiple arrests over the death of Brown, an unarmed black 18-year-old and other police shootings. The 2014 parade was supposed to be held several days after a St. Louis County grand jury decided to not indict former Ferguson police Officer Darren Wilson, who is white, in Brown's death. --In Illinois, after two days of demonstrations following the release of a video that shows a white Chicago police officer shooting and killing black teenager Laquan McDonald in 2014, protest organizers said there were no marches planned for Thanksgiving Day. Instead, they said they were preparing for a march through the city's famed shopping district, the Magnificent Mile, on Friday.
