PARIS >> Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets of France today as a vastly reinforced security presence appeared to have averted a repeat of last weekend’s unrest, despite isolated clashes in several cities. About 110,000 people marched peacefully through the French capital, according to police numbers. Waving flags, they denounced the growing cost of living and rising inequality. “Down with the state, the police and the fascists,” the crowd chanted. At the end of the march, police fired tear gas and used water cannon to try to disperse small groups of hooded youths, but the violence was far less than last Saturday, when looters and vandals went on the rampage in Paris. Clashes also flared in Lyon, Bordeaux and Grenoble, while police fired volleys of tear gas at demonstrators in Clermont-Ferrand, Lille and Nice. In France’s second city, Marseille, youths dragged large metal sheets to block a street, set fire to rubbish bins, and hurled rocks and bottles at riot police, with the confrontations continuing as night fell. Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE! The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in nationwide protests, while unions claimed turnout was double that. Authorities deployed 70,000 police officers and gendarmes, 10,000 more than a week earlier, after conceding they had underestimated the scale of the unrest. “We have to be ultra, ultra responsive,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters, accusing far-left activists and criminal gangs of seeking to foment violence. Nunez told reporters that police had arrested 135 people nationwide by early afternoon, many following pre-emptive searches that he said had uncovered fireworks, ball bearings and other items that could be used as weapons. Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers boarding up storefronts, museums closing their doors and more than 20 metro stations shut. Business groups urged retailers to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend. “There are hardly any customers, so it’s not really worth staying open,” said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris. Several of the capital’s best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musee d’Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated. “Everything’s boarded up and we’re not quite sure where we should be,” said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from New Orleans, Lousiana. The nationwide unrest began with small student demonstrations in suburban Paris last month to denounce school conditions. After it spread into a broader protest against the state of the economy in France, it also prompted demonstrators to take to the streets in neighbouring countries. Today, Belgian police used tear gas and pepper spray as they clashed in Brussels with anti-government demonstrators, while protests took place in Italian cities for a second weekend. Leftist leaders in France denounced a government move to limit the number of authorized marches in many cities, as well as a last-minute decision to shift the Paris event to the southeastern fringes of the capital. Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who joined the Paris rally, hailed what he called a “magnificent mass display of collective discipline and self-restraint”. He predicted the protests would continue until President Emmanuel Macron, whose mandate expires next year, addressed the social malaise in France, one of the world’s richest nations but with a growing debt mountain that has alarmed investors. “Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door,” Melenchon told reporters. Many demonstrators have accused the government of overreacting, as soldiers were dispatched to patrol the Champs-Elysees, a grand boulevard lined with luxury shops and restaurants. “We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round,” said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student. “My friend and I almost didn’t come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it’s important not to let repression win,” she added. The first authorised march today passed off peacefully in Orleans, around 75 miles south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally, which is holding a party congress in the city. A shooting west of Paris on Friday heightened tensions. A gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl. “We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid,” said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon’s France Unbowed party. 500 Ala Moana Blvd. #2-200 Honolulu, HI 96813 (808) 529-4747

sources.title: You can watch Instagram Reels on your TV now – these sets get the app first - ZDNET
passages: Amazon announced that, starting today, users can watch Reels on Fire TV devices with a dedicated app.
This is the first time Instagram content has been designed for television.
Like the mobile app, the TV app curates Reels into personalized channels based on your interests, like music, sports, travel, and trending moments.
You can search for content or scroll a stream, and you can see comments and reactions on screen while you scroll and even re-share Reels.
The app supports up to five accounts, Amazon explained, so everyone in a household can sign in and enjoy their own personalized experience.
You can also create a new account just for your TV if you want a whole family experience.

If the name sounds vaguely familiar, it’s because Instagram had an unrelated “IGTV” app for watching long-form content that debuted in 2018 and shut down in 2021.

sources.title: Instagram Launches on Apple TV, Expanding Video Experience with Reels and Live Shows
passages: The rollout of the Apple TV app aligns with these goals, as it includes not only Reels but also longer creator-driven content, episodic series, and live broadcasts—allowing for a more comprehensive viewing experience on a larger screen.

Users will require tvOS 26.0 or later to access the new Instagram app on Apple TV, which is now available on the App Store.
In related news, new details have surfaced regarding upcoming Apple products, including an unreleased Apple TV 4K.
The app's initial phase featured Reels sorted into channels that cater to user interests, facilitating a seamless autoplay experience.
The Instagram app is designed to enhance the viewing experience, enabling users to watch favorite creators' content and explore new videos.
This release follows Instagram's dedicated iPad app, which launched in September 2025, addressing long-standing user requests for an interface specifically optimized for Apple's tablets.
In June, Meta, Instagram's parent company, revealed intentions to evolve its content offerings beyond short-form videos.
Instagram promotes this app as a tool for friends and family to watch together, broadening its video-sharing capabilities beyond mobile screens.

extraction.body: Only tech companies are seeing growth from the AI boom, Apollo Global Management says. Apollo says that though some big companies are spending big on AI, they may soon pull back. Corporate America is starting to see AI spending not as a source of growth, but as a cost center. One of the world's largest investment firms says that only tech companies are getting a share of the AI pie . In an economic analysis published on Saturday, Apollo Global Management said that while the Magnificent Seven — a group of established tech companies that includes Nvidia and Meta — are seeing revenue growth during the AI boom, this growth isn't being shared by other industries. "Mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Torsten Slok, a partner and chief economist at Apollo, said in the report. "The technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech." In a series of graphs, Slok measured three main metrics that have boomed for tech companies but not for regular companies: revenue per worker, profit margins, and productivity growth. Since 2022, revenue per employee figures have skyrocketed for tech companies — rising from $550,000 to nearly $800,000 today. Meanwhile, that figure hasn't changed much for everyone else in the S&P 500, lingering around $550,000 for the last seven years. Similarly, while profit margins soared among tech companies since 2022, they've stagnated at about 10% for everyone else. And across the economy, AI hasn't yet dramatically increased productivity growth as some AI optimists have predicted. Apollo's research portends a dark shadow over a US economy throwing massive amounts of dough toward AI tools and companies, whose leaders have promised that an " age of abundance ," where people won't have to work as much, will soon be upon us. "The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins," Slok said. "That may be harder than it sounds," he added. If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

Torsten Slok's October 24 note found flat margins and revenue per worker across the S&P 493, even as Microsoft guides to $190 billion in 2026 AI capex and Meta plans up to $135 billion. Seven companies are carrying an AI boom that, by one economist's math, has yet to show up anywhere else in corporate America. That gap is now the central argument of the AI bubble skeptics. Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, published a note on October 24 making a specific, checkable claim: revenue per worker and profit margins have climbed for the Magnificent Seven since the AI spending wave began, and have stayed essentially flat for the other 493 companies in the S&P 500. Slok's own phrase for it, reported by Bloomberg, was that AI has delivered "zero payoff" to that broader group. Companies outside the Mag 7 are mentioning AI constantly on earnings calls, he found, but the mentions aren't translating into the numbers that are supposed to follow: faster revenue growth, fatter margins, or real cost savings. Slok's framing, also picked up by Fortune, is that mainstream corporate America is starting to treat AI token spending less like an investment and more like a cost center weighing on margins. That's a blunt reversal of the pitch every enterprise AI vendor has been selling for two years. If the companies buying the tools can't point to the return, the sales pitch has a hole in it. Here's why the distinction between the Mag 7 and the other 493 matters so much right now. Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet, Amazon and Nvidia are major sellers of AI chips, cloud capacity and related infrastructure, while all seven companies are investing heavily in AI. Microsoft reported $41 billion in capital spending in its latest quarter, up 70% from a year earlier, and said an accounting change would put its calendar-year 2026 guidance at roughly $175 billion while leaving the underlying investment plan unchanged. Meta has raised its 2026 capex guidance to $135 billion to $145 billion. Consensus estimates cited by Goldman Sachs put total 2026 capital spending by U.S. hyperscalers at about $800 billion, although not all of that spending is exclusively for AI. That's the spending side. Slok's aggregate charts show no comparable improvement in revenue per worker or profit margins among the other 493 companies. The comparison does not isolate AI's effect at individual companies or establish that AI caused the gap, but it shows that broad financial gains have yet to appear in those measures. CoreWeave's five-year CDS spread hit a record 1,194.5 basis points on October 15, implying roughly a 63% default probability, while Oracle's climbed near 300 basis points amid a $466 billion AI debt binge. - how AI company debt default risk is priced - CoreWeave credit default swap spread hits record high Slok's note landed less than two weeks after a sharper, faster scare in the market that funds the AI buildout. In mid-October, a chart about CoreWeave's debt load went viral on X after venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya flagged that the yield on $1.25 billion of the company's bonds due in 2032 had briefly touched 15%. CoreWeave, which is backed by Nvidia and had about $35 billion in debt plus roughly $16 billion in debt-like lease liabilities at the end of June, became a focal point for worries about AI financing. Its shares fell more than 15% on October 14, while yields on its unsecured bonds subsequently remained near 15%, as Oracle and several other AI infrastructure stocks also sold off. The CoreWeave scare was about leverage: a company borrowing heavily against future AI income it hasn't earned yet. Slok's note is a different and arguably more fundamental worry, about whether the income shows up at all once you look past the handful of companies both building and buying the infrastructure. Put those two stories next to each other and the AI trade starts to look like it's being carried by a very small number of balance sheets, both on the supply side and the demand side. Frankly, this is the number every founder selling an "AI productivity" tool into the enterprise should sit with. If S&P 500 companies with finance teams, procurement departments and CFOs under pressure to show ROI can't produce measurable gains from AI spending yet, that's a harder sell for a startup asking a mid-market customer to trust the same promise on a much smaller budget and a much shorter sales cycle. It doesn't mean the tools don't work. It means the case for them still runs on a story about the future, not a number from the last quarter. extraction.body: Only tech companies are seeing growth from the AI boom, Apollo Global Management says. Apollo says that though some big companies are spending big on AI, they may soon pull back. Corporate America is starting to see AI spending not as a source of growth, but as a cost center. One of the world's largest investment firms says that only tech companies are getting a share of the AI pie . In an economic analysis published on Saturday, Apollo Global Management said that while the Magnificent Seven — a group of established tech companies that includes Nvidia and Meta — are seeing revenue growth during the AI boom, this growth isn't being shared by other industries. "Mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Torsten Slok, a partner and chief economist at Apollo, said in the report. "The technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech." In a series of graphs, Slok measured three main metrics that have boomed for tech companies but not for regular companies: revenue per worker, profit margins, and productivity growth. Since 2022, revenue per employee figures have skyrocketed for tech companies — rising from $550,000 to nearly $800,000 today. Meanwhile, that figure hasn't changed much for everyone else in the S&P 500, lingering around $550,000 for the last seven years. Similarly, while profit margins soared among tech companies since 2022, they've stagnated at about 10% for everyone else. And across the economy, AI hasn't yet dramatically increased productivity growth as some AI optimists have predicted. Apollo's research portends a dark shadow over a US economy throwing massive amounts of dough toward AI tools and companies, whose leaders have promised that an " age of abundance ," where people won't have to work as much, will soon be upon us. "The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins," Slok said. "That may be harder than it sounds," he added. If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

Torsten Slok's October 24 note found flat margins and revenue per worker across the S&P 493, even as Microsoft guides to $190 billion in 2026 AI capex and Meta plans up to $135 billion. Seven companies are carrying an AI boom that, by one economist's math, has yet to show up anywhere else in corporate America. That gap is now the central argument of the AI bubble skeptics. Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, published a note on October 24 making a specific, checkable claim: revenue per worker and profit margins have climbed for the Magnificent Seven since the AI spending wave began, and have stayed essentially flat for the other 493 companies in the S&P 500. Slok's own phrase for it, reported by Bloomberg, was that AI has delivered "zero payoff" to that broader group. Companies outside the Mag 7 are mentioning AI constantly on earnings calls, he found, but the mentions aren't translating into the numbers that are supposed to follow: faster revenue growth, fatter margins, or real cost savings. Slok's framing, also picked up by Fortune, is that mainstream corporate America is starting to treat AI token spending less like an investment and more like a cost center weighing on margins. That's a blunt reversal of the pitch every enterprise AI vendor has been selling for two years. If the companies buying the tools can't point to the return, the sales pitch has a hole in it. Here's why the distinction between the Mag 7 and the other 493 matters so much right now. Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet, Amazon and Nvidia are major sellers of AI chips, cloud capacity and related infrastructure, while all seven companies are investing heavily in AI. Microsoft reported $41 billion in capital spending in its latest quarter, up 70% from a year earlier, and said an accounting change would put its calendar-year 2026 guidance at roughly $175 billion while leaving the underlying investment plan unchanged. Seven companies are carrying an AI boom that, by one economist's math, has yet to show up anywhere else in corporate America. That gap is now the central argument of the AI bubble skeptics.

Companies outside the Mag 7 are mentioning AI constantly on earnings calls, he found, but the mentions aren't translating into the numbers that are supposed to follow: faster revenue growth, fatter margins, or real cost savings.

Slok's framing, also picked up by Fortune, is that mainstream corporate America is starting to treat AI token spending less like an investment and more like a cost center weighing on margins. Over the last few months, it has become apparent that Google parent Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG) is Warren Buffett's favorite artificial intelligence (AI) stock. Although he retired from his role as CEO of Berkshire Hathaway at the end of 2025, he was the one who initiated its initial investment in the tech giant -- a stake that has grown into its third-largest equity holding under his successor, Greg Abel. Buffett has repeatedly stated that forever is his favorite holding period for an investment, and even now, he appears to retain his talent for finding such stocks. Thus, Berkshire's newest megastock is likely a good fit for individual portfolios as well, and two reasons explain why. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » For all of the hype about artificial intelligence (AI), Alphabet continues to earn most of its revenue from digital advertising. It began applying AI to its applications back in 2001. However, it has likely drawn more attention with Google Gemini, which seems to have answered the competitive threats from ChatGPT and Claude. Moreover, it has leveraged the technology to drive growth at Google Cloud, the platform through which it provides foundational models, developer tools, and infrastructure for AI, including support for Google Gemini. So successful is its approach that Google Cloud grew its revenue by 82% year over year in the second quarter of 2026. The Google parent has also leveraged AI through its autonomous driving subsidiary, Waymo. Its Waymo Driver platform utilizes AI as the foundation for autonomous driving, applying it to examine vehicles' surroundings, anticipate human actions, and navigate streets safely. These platforms allow Alphabet to benefit from AI from multiple sources. This makes it more likely that it will remain a market leader in the technology. Another attribute of Alphabet that likely attracted Buffett's attention was its financials. This goes far beyond its low valuation, though he likely appreciates the ability to buy the communications stock at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 17. He probably also likes that the company holds more than $242 billion in liquidity, up from $127 billion one year ago. Admittedly, the liquidity factor touches on an aspect of Alphabet that would probably make Buffett uncomfortable under most circumstances -- its capital expenditures. The company has said it intends to spend between $195 billion and $205 billion on capex this year alone, largely on the build-out of its AI data center infrastructure. Consequently, it increased its long-term debt to around $123 billion, far above the $46.5 billion in long-term debt it had on the balance sheet at the end of June 2025. Still, this spending is likely a major reason for Google Cloud's revenue growth and the company's 24% overall revenue increase. Moreover, it can likely afford this investment. Alphabet generated over $53 billion in free cash flow over the past four reported quarters. (That metric excludes capex spending.) Buffett often calls cash flows "owner earnings." This may have been his justification for overlooking Alphabet's massive capex spending, and could give retail investors a green light to invest as he does. All things considered, Alphabet seems to be Warren Buffett's favorite AI stock. The Google parent has successfully leveraged its AI prowess across platforms such as cloud computing and autonomous driving. Furthermore, it offers a reasonable valuation, liquidity, and strong free cash flows. Given Alphabet's potential for success and strong financials, this is one time that it might pay for average investors to follow in Buffett's footsteps. Over the last few months, it has become apparent that Google parent Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG) is Warren Buffett's favorite artificial intelligence (AI) stock. Although he retired from his role as CEO of Berkshire Hathaway at the end of 2025, he was the one who initiated its initial investment in the tech giant -- a stake that has grown into its third-largest equity holding under his successor, Greg Abel. Buffett has repeatedly stated that forever is his favorite holding period for an investment, and even now, he appears to retain his talent for finding such stocks. Thus, Berkshire's newest megastock is likely a good fit for individual portfolios as well, and two reasons explain why. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » For all of the hype about artificial intelligence (AI), Alphabet continues to earn most of its revenue from digital advertising. It began applying AI to its applications back in 2001. However, it has likely drawn more attention with Google Gemini, which seems to have answered the competitive threats from ChatGPT and Claude. Moreover, it has leveraged the technology to drive growth at Google Cloud, the platform through which it provides foundational models, developer tools, and infrastructure for AI, including support for Google Gemini. So successful is its approach that Google Cloud grew its revenue by 82% year over year in the second quarter of 2026. The Google parent has also leveraged AI through its autonomous driving subsidiary, Waymo. Its Waymo Driver platform utilizes AI as the foundation for autonomous driving, applying it to examine vehicles' surroundings, anticipate human actions, and navigate streets safely. These platforms allow Alphabet to benefit from AI from multiple sources. This makes it more likely that it will remain a market leader in the technology. Another attribute of Alphabet that likely attracted Buffett's attention was its financials. This goes far beyond its low valuation, though he likely appreciates the ability to buy the communications stock at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 17. Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) reported strong third-quarter results on Oct. 20. The company's artificial intelligence (AI) segment -- dubbed Super Intelligence (SI) -- was particularly impressive. SpaceX's total revenue grew 161% year over year to $14.6 billion, while SI revenue soared 830% year over year to $7.6 billion.

Even with a $608 million contribution from an acquisition that closed in August and boosted its SI unit, this business's growth during the period was impressive. The fact that SpaceX is experiencing such strong demand for AI is arguably a bullish sign for the broader AI industry. And for investors still looking for stocks to capitalize on the AI market, here are two that look particularly attractive following SpaceX's third-quarter update: Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

During the third quarter, SpaceX's capex in its SI business was $16.4 billion, up 245.5% year over year. At least some of that money is likely landing right in Nvidia's pockets, as SpaceX continues to expand its capacity to meet the high demand for AI compute. This isn't just speculation either.

SpaceX's management pointed out, among other things, that even older Nvidia systems, like the H100 GPU ( graphics processing unit ), are renting out at a premium compared to when they were new -- the H100 launched in 2022.

That says a lot about Nvidia, and it strongly suggests that newer systems, like the company's Vera Rubin architecture, are experiencing even higher demand. Further, SpaceX's CEO, Elon Musk , predicted a shortage of superintelligence compute that would last for some time.

If true, this would certainly benefit Nvidia, potentially granting the company even more pricing power. The bottom line is that while some people still expect the AI bubble to burst and take Nvidia down with it, there is significant evidence that AI infrastructure spending could continue to grow unabated for the foreseeable future. SpaceX gave us more data confirming that.

Meanwhile, Nvidia remains the undisputed leader in GPUs and has significantly expanded its portfolio. The company is well-positioned to tap into the massive demand for AI compute in the medium term and could deliver outstanding returns. In short, it's still not too late to invest in Nvidia, even after its amazing performance over the past five years.

CoreWeave also rents out AI compute capacity through a network of data centers. Some investors are skeptical of the company's prospects right now, but it isn't because sales growth hasn't been impressive. In the second quarter, CoreWeave's revenue increased by 112.5% year over year to $2.6 billion.

CoreWeave ended the period with a revenue backlog of $104 billion, up 245.5% year over year. And that didn't include the more than $25 billion in revenue backlog it recorded in the first few weeks of the third quarter.
However, CoreWeave is incurring significant debt to fund its AI ambitions, which is a meaningful risk investors will need to keep in mind, in addition to the company's customer concentration.

With that said, SpaceX's recent results and management commentary suggest that the kinds of services CoreWeave offers will remain in high demand for a while, which makes its debt-related problems much less concerning.

Consider, for instance, that Musk said that SpaceX could rent out AI compute capacity several times over if the company accepted every request. In other words, current demand significantly exceeds capacity. Also, SpaceX's CFO, Bret Johnsen, noted that "At current pricing, new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year."

These are incredibly bullish signs for CoreWeave. And they arguably justify the company spending fortunes to increase its compute capacity. The stock is a bit riskier due to the issues mentioned above. However, it could deliver outstanding returns over the next five years.

If true, this would certainly benefit Nvidia, potentially granting the company even more pricing power. The bottom line is that while some people still expect the AI bubble to burst and take Nvidia down with it, there is significant evidence that AI infrastructure spending could continue to grow unabated for the foreseeable future. SpaceX gave us more data confirming that.

Meanwhile, Nvidia remains the undisputed leader in GPUs and has significantly expanded its portfolio. The company is well-positioned to tap into the massive demand for AI compute in the medium term and could deliver outstanding returns. In short, it's still not too late to invest in Nvidia, even after its amazing performance over the past five years.

Some investors are skeptical of the company's prospects right now, but it isn't because sales growth hasn't been impressive. CoreWeave ended the period with a revenue backlog of $104 billion, up 245.5% year over year. And that didn’t include the more than $25 billion in revenue backlog it recorded in the first few weeks of the third quarter.

In other words, current demand significantly exceeds capacity. Also, SpaceX's CFO, Bret Johnsen, noted that "At current pricing, new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year."

These are incredibly bullish signs for CoreWeave. And they arguably justify the company spending fortunes to increase its compute capacity. The stock is a bit riskier due to the issues mentioned above. However, it could deliver outstanding returns over the next five years.

SpaceX's total revenue grew 161% year over year to $14.6 billion, while SI revenue soared 830% year over year to $7.6 billion. Even with a $608 million contribution from an acquisition that closed in August and boosted its SI unit, this business’s growth during the period was impressive. The fact that SpaceX is experiencing such strong demand for AI is arguably a bullish sign for the broader AI industry. And for investors still looking for stocks to capitalize on the AI market, here are two that look particularly attractive following SpaceX's third-quarter update: Nvidia ( NVDA -0.59% ) and CoreWeave ( CRWV -2.46% ) . During the third quarter, SpaceX's capex in its SI business was $16.4 billion, up 245.5% year over year. At least some of that money is likely landing right in Nvidia's pockets, as SpaceX continues to expand its capacity to meet the high demand for AI compute. This isn't just speculation either. SpaceX's management pointed out, among other things, that even older Nvidia systems, like the H100 GPU ( graphics processing unit ), are renting out at a premium compared to when they were new -- the H100 launched in 2022. That says a lot about Nvidia, and it strongly suggests that newer systems, like the company's Vera Rubin architecture, are experiencing even higher demand. Further, SpaceX's CEO, Elon Musk , predicted a shortage of superintelligence compute that would last for some time. If true, this would certainly benefit Nvidia, potentially granting the company even more pricing power. The bottom line is that while some people still expect the AI bubble to burst and take Nvidia down with it, there is significant evidence that AI infrastructure spending could continue to grow unabated for the foreseeable future. SpaceX gave us more data confirming that. Meanwhile, Nvidia remains the undisputed leader in GPUs and has significantly expanded its portfolio. The company is well-positioned to tap into the massive demand for AI compute in the medium term and could deliver outstanding returns. In short, it's still not too late to invest in Nvidia, even after its amazing performance over the past five years. CoreWeave also rents out AI compute capacity through a network of data centers. Some investors are skeptical of the company's prospects right now, but it isn't because sales growth hasn't been impressive. In the second quarter, CoreWeave's revenue increased by 112.5% year over year to $2.6 billion. CoreWeave ended the period with a revenue backlog of $104 billion, up 245.5% year over year. And that didn’t include the more than $25 billion in revenue backlog it recorded in the first few weeks of the third quarter. However, CoreWeave is incurring significant debt to fund its AI ambitions, which is a meaningful risk investors will need to keep in mind, in addition to the company's customer concentration. With that said, SpaceX's recent results and management commentary suggest that the kinds of services CoreWeave offers will remain in high demand for a while, which makes its debt-related problems much less concerning. Consider, for instance, that Musk said that SpaceX could rent out AI compute capacity several times over if the company accepted every request. In other words, current demand significantly exceeds capacity. Also, SpaceX's CFO, Bret Johnsen, noted that "At current pricing, new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year." These are incredibly bullish signs for CoreWeave. And they arguably justify the company spending fortunes to increase its compute capacity. The stock is a bit riskier due to the issues mentioned above. However, it could deliver outstanding returns over the next five years. Prosper Junior Bakiny has positions in Nvidia. extraction.body: Top 10% of firms account for 99.5% of AI inference spend in Ramp data cited by Apollo. Can the rest of corporate America turn cheap tokens into higher margins? Artificial intelligence has delivered no measurable financial return to US companies outside the technology sector, according to Torsten Slok, partner and chief economist at Apollo Global Management, in a Daily Spark note published on October 24, 2026. The note, titled No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector , sets five charts side by side: revenue per worker, profit margins, productivity growth, the concentration of AI spending and the financial backing of the heaviest AI buyers. Its conclusion is blunt. "Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech," Slok wrote. A top economist at the investment firm Apollo looked at whether ordinary big US companies, not the tech giants, are making more money because of AI, and found no sign that they are. This matters because the huge sums being poured into AI chips, data centres and models only make sense if the thousands of companies buying AI eventually earn more from it. For now, the data shows the gains staying with the biggest tech firms, while spending on AI services sits with a small group of mostly venture-backed companies. The note's central device is a division of the S&P 500 into two unequal parts. The "Mag 7" - the seven largest US technology companies, usually counted as Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla - sit on one side. The remaining 493 constituents, which Slok calls the "S&P 493," sit on the other. Apollo's note does not list the seven names; the grouping is the conventional one used across financial markets. "Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493," Slok wrote. "Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493." The first chart, titled "Revenue per worker moving up for tech but not for the rest of the economy," tracks inflation-adjusted revenue per employee, in thousands of dollars at 2019 fourth-quarter prices, from the first quarter of 2019. On PPC Land's reading of the chart, the Magnificent 7 started the period at roughly $695,000 per employee, fell to a trough of about $565,000 around the turn of 2022 and 2023, and then climbed steadily to roughly $780,000 in the most recent quarter shown, with the sharpest jump at the very end of the series. The S&P 493 line moves within a much narrower band: about $495,000 in early 2019, a low near $465,000 in 2021, a peak around $548,000 in late 2022, and roughly $527,000 in the latest reading. Apollo credits Bloomberg, Macrobond and its own chief economist's office for the data. The second chart, "No signs of profit margins going up outside the tech sector," goes back further, to the first quarter of 2015. Reading from Apollo's chart, the Magnificent 7 profit margin rose from around 11% in 2015 to about 22% in early 2022, dropped to roughly 14% in 2023, and has since risen to close to 30%. The S&P 493 margin stood at about 8.5% in 2015, dipped to around 6.5% during the pandemic, peaked near 11.7% in early 2022, and has hovered between 9% and 10% since 2023. These figures are approximations taken from the plotted lines; Apollo did not publish the underlying values in the note. The shape matters as much as the level. For the largest technology companies, both revenue per worker and margins have accelerated in the period that coincides with heavy AI investment. For the rest of the index, the lines are close to flat over the same years. The third chart widens the lens from corporate accounts to the whole economy. Titled "No signs of AI boosting productivity growth," it plots two measures of year-over-year productivity growth from January 1985: labour output per hour from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, and total factor productivity, or TFP. The TFP series is the utilisation-adjusted measure maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (Fernald, 2014), which corrects for cyclical swings in how intensively capital and labour are used. On the chart, output per hour spiked to around 7% during the 2020 pandemic, when lower-productivity jobs disappeared first, and then dipped below zero. In the most recent readings, output per hour growth runs at roughly 2% to 2.5%, while TFP growth has slipped to around zero and appears slightly negative at the end of the series. Neither line shows the kind of sustained step up that would mark a technology-driven productivity boom. "There are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth," Slok wrote. TFP is the measure economists usually watch for the effect of a general-purpose technology, because it captures output growth that cannot be explained by adding more workers or more machines. A flat or falling TFP line, set against record AI capital spending, is the core of Slok's case. The note goes further than describing flat lines. It makes a claim about corporate behaviour. "With no impact on the bottom line, mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Slok wrote. Token spending refers to the fees companies pay to AI providers for processing text and data, measured in tokens . The note does not quantify the pullback it describes, and it does not cite a survey for the shift in attitude. Other recent data points in the same direction. A KPMG survey of 2,145 senior leaders found that 49% had scaled back, narrowed, delayed or paused AI agent rollouts after costs began to outweigh value, while only 7% reported established return on investment. An August TransUnion study found that 53% of enterprise marketers reported meaningful ROI from AI, with most gains so far coming from time savings rather than revenue. Slok also draws a line between who buys AI and who does not. "VC-backed companies are spending more and more on tokens, but mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it," he wrote. Artificial intelligence has delivered no measurable financial return to US companies outside the technology sector, according to Torsten Slok, partner and chief economist at Apollo Global Management, in a Daily Spark note published on October 24, 2026. The note, titled No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector , sets five charts side by side: revenue per worker, profit margins, productivity growth, the concentration of AI spending and the financial backing of the heaviest AI buyers. Its conclusion is blunt. "Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech," Slok wrote.

A top economist at the investment firm Apollo looked at whether ordinary big US companies, not the tech giants, are making more money because of AI, and found no sign that they are. This matters because the huge sums being poured into AI chips, data centres and models only make sense if the thousands of companies buying AI eventually earn more from it. For now, the data shows the gains staying with the biggest tech firms, while spending on AI services sits with a small group of mostly venture-backed companies.

The note's central device is a division of the S&P 500 into two unequal parts. The "Mag 7" - the seven largest US technology companies, usually counted as Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla - sit on one side. The remaining 493 constituents, which Slok calls the "S&P 493," sit on the other. Apollo's note does not list the seven names; the grouping is the conventional one used across financial markets.

The S&P 493 line moves within a much narrower band: about $495,000 in early 2019, a low near $465,000 in 2021, a peak around $548,000 in late 2022, and roughly $527,000 in the latest reading. Apollo credits Bloomberg, Macrobond and its own chief economist's office for the data.

The second chart, "No signs of profit margins going up outside the tech sector," goes back further, to the first quarter of 2015. Reading from Apollo's chart, the Magnificent 7 profit margin rose from around 11% in 2015 to about 22% in early 2022, dropped to roughly 14% in 2023, and has since risen to close to 30%. The S&P 493 margin stood at about 8.5% in 2015, dipped to around 6.5% during the pandemic, peaked near 11.7% in early 2022, and has hovered between 9% and 10% since 2023. These figures are approximations taken from the plotted lines; Apollo did not publish the underlying values in the note.

The shape matters as much as the level. For the largest technology companies, both revenue per worker and margins have accelerated in the period that coincides with heavy AI investment. For the rest of the index, the lines are close to flat over the same years.

The TFP series is the utilisation-adjusted measure maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (Fernald, 2014), which corrects for cyclical swings in how intensively capital and labour are used.

On the chart, output per hour spiked to around 7% during the 2020 pandemic, when lower-productivity jobs disappeared first, and then dipped below zero. In the most recent readings, output per hour growth runs at roughly 2% to 2.5%, while TFP growth has slipped to around zero and appears slightly negative at the end of the series. Neither line shows the kind of sustained step up that would mark a technology-driven productivity boom. "There are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth," Slok wrote.

TFP is the measure economists usually watch for the effect of a general-purpose technology, because it captures output growth that cannot be explained by adding more workers or more machines. A flat or falling TFP line, set against record AI capital spending, is the core of Slok's case.

Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech. Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493, see the first chart below. Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493, see the second chart below. And there are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth, see the third chart below. With no impact on the bottom line, mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins.

VC-backed companies are spending more and more on tokens, but mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it. As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited, see the fourth and fifth charts below.

The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins. That may be harder than it sounds. AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment. Judgment depends on context, and the answer varies with which human or which model you ask. Perhaps most importantly, AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.
The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector.

coreStoryFacts.text: What: A Daily Spark note arguing that AI has delivered "zero financial payoff" to US companies outside tech.

Revenue per worker and profit margins have risen for the Magnificent 7 but stayed flat for the S&P 493, productivity growth shows no AI effect, the top 10% of firms account for 99.5% of model serving and inference spend in Ramp data, and 80.4% of the top 1% of AI spenders are venture-backed.
The second chart, "No signs of profit margins going up outside the tech sector," goes back further, to the first quarter of 2015.
These figures are approximations taken from the plotted lines; Apollo did not publish the underlying values in the note.
Apollo credits Bloomberg, Macrobond and its own chief economist's office for the data.
The October 24 note is the latest in a run of Daily Spark entries in which Slok has tracked the gap between AI investment and returns outside technology.
The "Mag 7" - the seven largest US technology companies, usually counted as Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla - sit on one side.
Apollo's note does not list the seven names; the grouping is the conventional one used across financial markets.
When their margins are flat, marketing budgets come under the same scrutiny Slok describes for token spending.
Many of the AI features built into ad platforms - automated bidding, generated creative, agentic AI tools that run campaigns - are sold to these buyers on the promise of efficiency.
The charts show correlation in time, not cause.

Rising Magnificent 7 margins could reflect AI-driven sales of cloud capacity, chips and advertising, but they also reflect cost cutting, layoffs, pricing power and cyclical factors that predate the current wave of generative AI.
The implication is that a large share of measured AI demand comes from companies whose spending depends on fresh capital rather than on operating profits.
The fourth and fifth charts carry that argument with spending data from Ramp, the corporate card and expense management company, which publishes the Ramp AI Index based on business transaction data.
The fourth chart, titled "AI spending is extremely concentrated in a small number of firms," is a table credited to Ara Kharazian, chief economist at Ramp, and Apollo's chief economist.
Can the rest of corporate America turn cheap tokens into higher margins?
A top economist at the investment firm Apollo looked at whether ordinary big US companies, not the tech giants, are making more money because of AI, and found no sign that they are.
This matters because the huge sums being poured into AI chips, data centres and models only make sense if the thousands of companies buying AI eventually earn more from it.
For now, the data shows the gains staying with the biggest tech firms, while spending on AI services sits with a small group of mostly venture-backed companies.
Ray Dalio said earlier this month that his bubble indicator puts AI level with 1929 and 2000 .

Analyst Ed Zitron argued in August, citing UBS estimates, that OpenAI and Anthropic could make up more than 48% of Google Cloud revenue in 2027 - a concentration risk that echoes the Ramp data in Slok's note.
When: Published October 24, 2026, following related Apollo notes on June 30 and August 9, 2026.
Where: The United States, with the analysis centred on S&P 500 companies and Ramp's business spending data.

extraction.body: Top 10% of firms account for 99.5% of AI inference spend in Ramp data cited by Apollo. Can the rest of corporate America turn cheap tokens into higher margins? Artificial intelligence has delivered no measurable financial return to US companies outside the technology sector, according to Torsten Slok, partner and chief economist at Apollo Global Management, in a Daily Spark note published on October 24, 2026. The note, titled No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector , sets five charts side by side: revenue per worker, profit margins, productivity growth, the concentration of AI spending and the financial backing of the heaviest AI buyers. This raises the question: Is Cardano fundamentally undervalued, or is the market correctly assessing its worth? Market capitalization, calculated by multiplying the number of coins in circulation by their current price, places Ethereum as the second-largest cryptocurrency, with Cardano at 18th. See for yourself by clicking here now. (Sponsor) In theory, a smaller market cap like Cardano's could signal growth potential because it requires less new investment to raise its price. However, this hasn't held true recently. Over the past year, ETH fell 40.4%, while ADA fell even more, 68.1%. Over five years, ETH lost 43.2%, while ADA fell 90.3%. Each time the market turned down, Cardano lost more ground, suggesting investors view ADA as riskier. Market cap calculations have their limitations. They value assets based on the most recent trade price, so trading activity in a thin market can drive price volatility. Trading volume better reflects market depth, with Ethereum seeing about $8.4 billion in trades in the last 24 hours compared to just $213.7 million for Cardano. However, a significant portion of trading volume comes from automated programs known as market-making bots, which facilitate buying and selling throughout the day. Despite this, Ethereum's deeper market allows larger investors to trade without significantly impacting the price, attracting institutional investment. Another factor to consider is supply dilution—this occurs when new coins enter circulation. About 37.6 billion ADA are in circulation out of a maximum of 45 billion, giving a fully diluted valuation (the value if all coins were trading) of about $9.2 billion. In contrast, Ethereum's fully diluted value matches its market cap, making Cardano more susceptible to future supply increases. Ethereum also benefits from regulatory approval. As of October 22, U.S. spot Ethereum ETFs, which are funds that hold ETH and trade similarly to stocks, collectively managed $14.6 billion in assets, with a significant $12.7 billion in net inflows. Cardano, on the other hand, lacks a similar financial instrument. Grayscale withdrew its application for a Cardano Trust ETF on August 7, and that was the only dedicated U.S. spot ADA product in progress. Ethereum's lead is also bolstered by network effects, meaning that as more users join the Ethereum network, its usefulness increases. Most stablecoins (tokens pegged to the U.S. dollar), DeFi applications (financial services operating on code), and tokenized funds are built on Ethereum. New projects tend to gravitate toward the more established network, further widening the usage gap. On both networks, most transactions occur on exchanges and don't reach the blockchain, so a quieter Cardano network may suggest buyers are accumulating ADA or hesitating to buy—on-chain data can't clarify the situation. The market gap could narrow on Ethereum's side. On October 22, Ethereum ETFs reported a net outflow of $110.5 million, with the largest single-day outflow recently reaching $201.9 million on October 6. Cumulative inflows have decreased from $14.0 billion to $12.7 billion since September 28. On the Cardano side, the network supported the SEC's proposed "Regulation Crypto Assets" in a comment letter, as reported on October 21. Although this shows support, it has little immediate effect. The regulation could help ADA's price if it simplifies launching new U.S. products—assuming a sponsor eventually steps forward to file one. On October 21, Cardano's founder, Charles Hoskinson, welcomed TRON (CRYPTO:TRX) to Midnight (CRYPTO:NIGHT), Cardano's privacy-focused partner chain, with the integration expected in December. However, payments from that collaboration would benefit Midnight first and reach ADA only indirectly. Yet, Hoskinson has faced scrutiny over a new programming language he says he is developing for Cardano, which lacks a technical specification. This has sparked skepticism in the community, making it clear that Cardano faces both challenges and opportunities ahead. We don't expect the significant 37.2x gap between Ethereum (ETH) and Cardano (ADA) to close much. The Fear reading of 40 suggests investors are pricing Cardano appropriately, since ADA hasn't attracted significant new funds. For those holding ADA, the challenge is that the coin has dropped 68.1% over the past year and could continue to lag behind ETH. For Cardano to close this gap, it would likely need a strong push. This could come from a new spot ADA exchange-traded fund (ETF) that attracts investment, or from stablecoin projects or tokenized funds choosing to use its blockchain. Unfortunately, Cardano has yet to see any of these developments. A key price point to watch is ADA rising above $0.26, which was its value on September 25. While Cardano has shown stronger growth in certain periods, increasing by 34.0% over the last 90 days compared to Ethereum's 24.6% increase, it has faced recent challenges.
This raises the question: Is Cardano fundamentally undervalued, or is the market correctly assessing its worth?
Ethereum's $285 billion market cap dwarfs Cardano's $7.7 billion, with ETH's daily trading volume of $8.4 billion versus ADA's $214 million.
We don't expect the significant 37.2x gap between Ethereum (ETH) and Cardano (ADA) to close much.
Market capitalization, calculated by multiplying the number of coins in circulation by their current price, places Ethereum as the second-largest cryptocurrency, with Cardano at 18th.

However, this hasn't held true recently. Over the past year, ETH fell 40.4%, while ADA fell even more, 68.1%. Over five years, ETH lost 43.2%, while ADA fell 90.3%. Each time the market turned down, Cardano lost more ground, suggesting investors view ADA as riskier. Market cap calculations have their limitations. They value assets based on the most recent trade price, so trading activity in a thin market can drive price volatility. Trading volume better reflects market depth, with Ethereum seeing about $8.4 billion in trades in the last 24 hours compared to just $213.7 million for Cardano. However, a significant portion of trading volume comes from automated programs known as market-making bots, which facilitate buying and selling throughout the day. Despite this, Ethereum's deeper market allows larger investors to trade without significantly impacting the price, attracting institutional investment. Another factor to consider is supply dilution—this occurs when new coins enter circulation. About 37.6 billion ADA are in circulation out of a maximum of 45 billion, giving a fully diluted valuation (the value if all coins were trading) of about $9.2 billion. In contrast, Ethereum's fully diluted value matches its market cap, making Cardano more susceptible to future supply increases. Ethereum also benefits from regulatory approval. Ethereum's lead is also bolstered by network effects, meaning that as more users join the Ethereum network, its usefulness increases. Most stablecoins (tokens pegged to the U.S. dollar), DeFi applications (financial services operating on code), and tokenized funds are built on Ethereum. New projects tend to gravitate toward the more established network, further widening the usage gap. On both networks, most transactions occur on exchanges and don't reach the blockchain, so a quieter Cardano network may suggest buyers are accumulating ADA or hesitating to buy—on-chain data can't clarify the situation. The market gap could narrow on Ethereum's side. On October 22, Ethereum ETFs reported a net outflow of $110.5 million, with the largest single-day outflow recently reaching $201.9 million on October 6. On the Cardano side, the network supported the SEC's proposed "Regulation Crypto Assets" in a comment letter, as reported on October 21. Although this shows support, it has little immediate effect. The regulation could help ADA's price if it simplifies launching new U.S. products—assuming a sponsor eventually steps forward to file one. On October 21, Cardano's founder, Charles Hoskinson, welcomed TRON (CRYPTO:TRX) to Midnight (CRYPTO:NIGHT), Cardano's privacy-focused partner chain, with the integration expected in December. However, payments from that collaboration would benefit Midnight first and reach ADA only indirectly. Yet, Hoskinson has faced scrutiny over a new programming language he says he is developing for Cardano, which lacks a technical specification. This has sparked skepticism in the community, making it clear that Cardano faces both challenges and opportunities ahead. We don't expect the significant 37.2x gap between Ethereum (ETH) and Cardano (ADA) to close much. The Fear reading of 40 suggests investors are pricing Cardano appropriately, since ADA hasn't attracted significant new funds. For those holding ADA, the challenge is that the coin has dropped 68.1% over the past year and could continue to lag behind ETH. For Cardano to close this gap, it would likely need a strong push. This could come from a new spot ADA exchange-traded fund (ETF) that attracts investment, or from stablecoin projects or tokenized funds choosing to use its blockchain. Unfortunately, Cardano has yet to see any of these developments. A key price point to watch is ADA rising above $0.26, which was its value on September 25. JPMorgan Chase ( NYSE: JPM ) has made headlines by placing nearly $900 million in tokenized funds on both Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) and Solana (CRYPTO: SOL). A tokenized fund is an investment fund whose shares exist as tokens on a blockchain, allowing them to trade around the clock.

According to Sentora data, the JPMorgan OnChain Liquidity-Token Money Market Fund (JLTXX) holds about $792 million across both networks, while the My OnChain Net Yield Fund (MONY) holds an estimated $103.1 million on Ethereum alone.

In just one week, JPMorgan took two significant steps. On October 19, 2026, Kinexys, the bank's blockchain unit, introduced its JPM Coin deposit token (JPMD) to Ethereum. Shortly after, on October 22, J.P. Morgan Asset Management launched MONY and JLTXX on Solana. However, despite these announcements, both cryptocurrencies saw declines: ETH fell to $2,333, down 2.1% for the week, while SOL dropped to $101, down 1.5%.

JLTXX is a U.S.-registered government money market fund that invests cash in short-term government debt and passes interest earnings directly to investors. JPMorgan designed it so that stablecoin issuers can hold reserves in JLTXX tokens under the GENIUS Act, a federal stablecoin law. JPMorgan first launched JLTXX on Ethereum in May.

SoFi Active Invest is offering a limited-time promotion. Open an account, fund it with $50 or more, and you could receive up to $1,000 in complimentary stock for Active Invest accounts. See for yourself by clicking here now. (Sponsor)

MONY, by contrast, is a private placement regulated under the SEC's Rule 506(c), meaning only high-net-worth individuals can invest. JPMorgan rolled this fund out in December 2025. Both funds operate through Morgan Money, JPMorgan's cash management platform, allowing investors to subscribe and redeem, then receive tokens at a designated blockchain address. Retail traders cannot purchase these tokens on exchanges.

Meanwhile, JPMD is a deposit token representing a dollar held in a JPMorgan bank account, enabling institutional clients to transact at any time. It initially launched on Base, the blockchain connected to Coinbase ( NASDAQ: COIN ), where Sentora reports a $1 million supply, but it is not yet available on Ethereum.

These tokenized funds bring in modest revenue compared to JPMorgan's core businesses. Fees from these funds contribute to Asset & Wealth Management, which manages over $5.1 trillion in client assets, while payments revenue, including JPMD, grew 12% in the second quarter. Additionally, neither Sentora nor JPMorgan has disclosed how JLTXX's $792 million is split between Ethereum and Solana, making it hard to say Solana has a significant share.

The announcements did not commit anyone to buy or hold ETH or SOL. When a tokenized fund moves its assets, it incurs small transaction fees known as gas. However, money market fund tokens mainly sit in a few institutional wallets, so they generate far less fee activity than stablecoin transfers or trading.

The Solana announcement notably excluded details about the on-chain cash used to trade the fund tokens. It mentioned Morgan Money as the subscription channel but did not reference any stablecoin or JPMD for Solana. Until JPMorgan identifies an on-chain cash option for Solana, the bank's own dollars will remain absent from that chain.

When explaining its choice of Ethereum, JPMorgan cited its "established depth of on-chain liquidity and tokenized assets," yet Sentora still shows no JPMD supply on Ethereum. Paul Przybylski, who leads digital and tokenized assets at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, said clients operate across multiple networks, so their liquidity should reflect that need. However, he did not provide specific figures to back that demand.

JPMorgan's timing on Solana also could be considered late, as competitors like BlackRock ( NYSE: BLK ) and Franklin Templeton introduced tokenized funds there in 2025. Currently, the market appears to be contracting, with Sentora reporting $14.4 billion in tokenized Treasury and money market products across 119 offerings, a 3.5% decline over the past month.

Ethereum currently leads JPMorgan's tokenized funds. MONY's $103.1 million is entirely Ethereum-based, JLTXX launched there first, and JPMD integrated into Ethereum before any other chain besides Base. Because Base is an Ethereum layer-2 network, the $1 million JPMD supply also links back to Ethereum.

JPMorgan and the respective coins gain different advantages from this move. JPMorgan stands to benefit from fee-generating fund assets and a reserve product tailored for stablecoin issuers, while Ethereum and Solana gain enhanced credibility and the potential for increased stablecoin and trading activity stemming from involvement with a prominent bank like JPMorgan. While both networks use a portion of their fees for validator rewards, the flow is negligible at these fund sizes.

For now, Ethereum appears to benefit more from JPMorgan's tokenized funds, though neither asset has guaranteed buyers. ETH has declined 12.5% over the past month, while SOL's value has fallen 16.1%, trends that far outweigh the impact of a few hundred million dollars in funds.

Solana could gain ground if JPMorgan names it as a JPMD network, giving the funds an on-chain cash option there, or if a Solana-based stablecoin issuer starts holding its reserves in JLTXX. If JPMD's Ethereum supply rises above zero before JPMorgan announces anything for Solana, Ethereum's lead likely holds, but a Solana JPMD launch first could start shifting the advantage to SOL.

However, money market fund tokens mainly sit in a few institutional wallets, so they generate far less fee activity than stablecoin transfers or trading.

The Solana announcement notably excluded details about the on-chain cash used to trade the fund tokens. However, he did not provide specific figures to back that demand.

While both networks use a portion of their fees for validator rewards, the flow is negligible at these fund sizes.

For now, Ethereum appears to benefit more from JPMorgan's tokenized funds, though neither asset has guaranteed buyers. ETH has declined 12.5% over the past month, while SOL's value has fallen 16.1%, trends that far outweigh the impact of a few hundred million dollars in funds.

passages: JPMorgan just parked nearly $900 million in tokenized funds across Ethereum and Solana, but the fine print reveals one chain got a much bigger piece of the deal than the headlines suggest.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

JPMorgan Chase ( NYSE: JPM | JPM Price Prediction ) has made headlines by placing nearly $900 million in tokenized funds on both Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ) and Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ). A tokenized fund is an investment fund whose shares exist as tokens on a blockchain, allowing them to trade around the clock.

According to Sentora data, the JPMorgan OnChain Liquidity-Token Money Market Fund (JLTXX) holds about $792 million across both networks, while the My OnChain Net Yield Fund (MONY) holds an estimated $103.1 million on Ethereum alone.

In just one week, JPMorgan took two significant steps. On October 19, 2026, Kinexys, the bank’s blockchain unit, introduced its JPM Coin deposit token (JPMD) to Ethereum. Shortly after, on October 22, J.P. Morgan Asset Management launched MONY and JLTXX on Solana. However, despite these announcements, both cryptocurrencies saw declines: ETH fell to $2,333, down 2.1% for the week, while SOL dropped to $101, down 1.5%.

JLTXX is a U.S.-registered government money market fund that invests cash in short-term government debt and passes interest earnings directly to investors. JPMorgan designed it so that stablecoin issuers can hold reserves in JLTXX tokens under the GENIUS Act, a federal stablecoin law. JPMorgan first launched JLTXX on Ethereum in May.

MONY, by contrast, is a private placement regulated under the SEC’s Rule 506(c), meaning only high-net-worth individuals can invest. JPMorgan rolled this fund out in December 2025. Both funds operate through Morgan Money, JPMorgan’s cash management platform, allowing investors to subscribe and redeem, then receive tokens at a designated blockchain address. Retail traders cannot purchase these tokens on exchanges.

Meanwhile, JPMD is a deposit token representing a dollar held in a JPMorgan bank account, enabling institutional clients to transact at any time. It initially launched on Base, the blockchain connected to Coinbase ( NASDAQ: COIN ), where Sentora reports a $1 million supply, but it is not yet available on Ethereum.

These tokenized funds bring in modest revenue compared to JPMorgan’s core businesses. Fees from these funds contribute to Asset & Wealth Management, which manages over $5.1 trillion in client assets, while payments revenue, including JPMD, grew 12% in the second quarter. Additionally, neither Sentora nor JPMorgan has disclosed how JLTXX’s $792 million is split between Ethereum and Solana, making it hard to say Solana has a significant share.

The announcements did not commit anyone to buy or hold ETH or SOL. When a tokenized fund moves its assets, it incurs small transaction fees known as gas. However, money market fund tokens mainly sit in a few institutional wallets, so they generate far less fee activity than stablecoin transfers or trading.

The Solana announcement notably excluded details about the on-chain cash used to trade the fund tokens. It mentioned Morgan Money as the subscription channel but did not reference any stablecoin or JPMD for Solana. Until JPMorgan identifies an on-chain cash option for Solana, the bank’s own dollars will remain absent from that chain.

When explaining its choice of Ethereum, JPMorgan cited its “established depth of on-chain liquidity and tokenized assets,” yet Sentora still shows no JPMD supply on Ethereum. Paul Przybylski, who leads digital and tokenized assets at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, said clients operate across multiple networks, so their liquidity should reflect that need. However, he did not provide specific figures to back that demand.

JPMorgan’s timing on Solana also could be considered late, as competitors like BlackRock ( NYSE: BLK ) and Franklin Templeton introduced tokenized funds there in 2025. Currently, the market appears to be contracting, with Sentora reporting $14.4 billion in tokenized Treasury and money market products across 119 offerings, a 3.5% decline over the past month.

Ethereum currently leads JPMorgan’s tokenized funds. MONY’s $103.1 million is entirely Ethereum-based, JLTXX launched there first, and JPMD integrated into Ethereum before any other chain besides Base. Because Base is an Ethereum layer-2 network, the $1 million JPMD supply also links back to Ethereum.

JPMorgan and the respective coins gain different advantages from this move. JPMorgan stands to benefit from fee-generating fund assets and a reserve product tailored for stablecoin issuers, while Ethereum and Solana gain enhanced credibility and the potential for increased stablecoin and trading activity stemming from involvement with a prominent bank like JPMorgan. While both networks use a portion of their fees for validator rewards , the flow is negligible at these fund sizes.

For now, Ethereum appears to benefit more from JPMorgan’s tokenized funds, though neither asset has guaranteed buyers. ETH has declined 12.5% over the past month, while SOL’s value has fallen 16.1%, trends that far outweigh the impact of a few hundred million dollars in funds.

Solana could gain ground if JPMorgan names it as a JPMD network, giving the funds an on-chain cash option there, or if a Solana-based stablecoin issuer starts holding its reserves in JLTXX. If JPMD’s Ethereum supply rises above zero before JPMorgan announces anything for Solana, Ethereum’s lead likely holds, but a Solana JPMD launch first could start shifting the advantage to SOL.

His analysis is syndicated on Yahoo Finance, MSN and AOL and has been cited by other crypto news sites.
He also founded MacLabs Marketing, a content and personal branding agency for crypto founders and executives.

ETF buyers previously positioned to defend the $80,000 floor turned sellers on October 22, while long positions near $81,993 add to the strain.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) slipped below key…
Bitcoin last traded at or below $77,600 on September 18, so what caused this dip, and how much further could it fall?
According to Glassnode data, the cost basis for spot ETF holders and treasury companies—public firms holding Bitcoin on their balance sheets—falls between $80,000 and $81,500.
Bitcoin's plunge below $80,000 triggered nearly a billion dollars in liquidations and set off alarm bells across global markets.
This decline followed a sharper drop the day before, when Bitcoin sank to $79,220 on Binance, marking weekly lows at $79,107, its weakest point in over a month.
Glassnode warned in its October 14 report that the largest buy orders on Binance were clustered around $80,000.
However, the dip occurred on relatively low trading volume compared to the October 24 selloff and quickly reversed, indicating a lack of strong conviction.
Bitcoin keeps slipping below a price level that its largest holders paid to get in, and a specific cluster of leveraged bets sits just overhead, ready to make any recovery harder than it looks.
Currently, Bitcoin is trading below both its 50-day average of $81,798 and its 20-day average of $82,539, suggesting that many recent buyers are now at a loss, giving short-term sellers an advantage.

Reports on October 24 indicated that the U.S. was rapidly evacuating personnel from embassies and military bases across the Middle East, citing intelligence about potential attacks by Iran on Americans.
Additionally, comments from the President at a Florida rally on October 23 hinted that tensions with Iran might escalate again after the midterms.

Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) has once again fallen below $80,000, briefly hitting $79,973 before buyers stepped in and pushed it back up to $80,287. This decline followed a sharper drop the day before, when Bitcoin sank to $79,220 on Binance, marking weekly lows at $79,107, its weakest point in over a month.

While this drop may seem limited, Bitcoin is down 3.3% for October but still up 26.8% over the last 90 days; the $80,000 threshold matters to its largest holders. Bitcoin last traded at or below $77,600 on September 18, so what caused this dip, and how much further could it fall?

External factors largely drove the downturn. Reports on October 24 indicated that the U.S. was rapidly evacuating personnel from embassies and military bases across the Middle East, citing intelligence about potential attacks by Iran on Americans. Additionally, comments from the President at a Florida rally on October 23 hinted that tensions with Iran might escalate again after the midterms.

As stock and bond markets close on weekends, investors often sell cryptocurrency to reduce risk, and Bitcoin is typically the most liquid option. Concerns about rising oil prices—West Texas Intermediate crude reached $107.89 a barrel on October 20, a spike of 13.1% in just a week—fueled inflation worries.

Further compounding the situation, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw a staggering net outflow of $635.5 million on October 22, the largest daily outflow since June, erasing the $528.4 million influx from the day before.

Interest rates don’t seem to be the primary driver of this drop. On October 22, the 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.96% from 5.31% earlier in the month, and lower yields usually support Bitcoin. Meanwhile, the VIX, a measure of expected stock market volatility, rose from 14.84 to 19.03, indicating growing apprehension among stock investors.

Leveraged traders could deepen the current downturn. Coinbase ( NASDAQ: COIN | COIN Price Prediction ) noted that the largest cluster of net long Bitcoin positions—trades made with borrowed money that profit from rising prices—averaged at $81,993, with 64% of their dollar value entered at prices above where Bitcoin currently trades.

Liquidation occurs when an exchange must forcibly close a borrowed position because significant losses consume the trader’s collateral. Each liquidation triggers a market sale that can drive further price drops, creating a chain reaction that continues until all over-leveraged positions are cleared. This type of selling often happens quickly and doesn’t necessarily reflect real demand.
Currently, Bitcoin is trading below both its 50-day average of $81,798 and its 20-day average of $82,539, suggesting that many recent buyers are now at a loss, giving short-term sellers an advantage.

Cost basis, or the average price paid by a group of investors, is crucial here. According to Glassnode data, the cost basis for spot ETF holders and treasury companies—public firms holding Bitcoin on their balance sheets—falls between $80,000 and $81,500. A decline below $80,000 could push this group, including ETF buyers who put $6.3 billion into ETFs in Q3 alone, into paper losses.

Glassnode warned in its October 14 report that the largest buy orders on Binance were clustered around $80,000. A close below this ETF cost basis could eliminate the nearest support identified in Bitcoin’s on-chain data. However, the dip occurred on relatively low trading volume compared to the October 24 selloff and quickly reversed, indicating a lack of strong conviction.
Bitcoin has dropped just 3.9%, while Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ) has fallen 12.5% and Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ) has lost 16.1%.

This resilience may stem from Bitcoin’s broader base of long-term buyers, as ETFs and treasury companies hold significant amounts near their cost basis and have an incentive to defend it. In contrast, Ethereum and Solana operate in smaller markets where leveraged trading plays a larger role, and investors tend to sell riskier assets first during periods of uncertainty.

If Bitcoin cannot reclaim $81,500, $77,600 appears to be the next significant level to watch. This target aligns with Glassnode’s True Market Mean—the average price paid by active investors, excluding coins that have remained inactive for years—and sits about 3.3% below the current price. ETF buyers previously positioned to defend the $80,000 floor turned sellers on October 22, while long positions near $81,993 add to the strain.
The outcome hinges on investor sentiment and external factors affecting the market.
