( NASDAQ: MSTR | MSTR Price Prediction ) experienced an $8.3 billion paper loss on its Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) holdings in the second quarter, largely due to a drop in the cryptocurrency’s price. The company is expected to announce its Q3 earnings on October 29, 2026, though it has not yet been officially confirmed. The big question now is whether Strategy can turn that significant loss into a third-quarter profit.

In its second-quarter report released on July 30, Strategy reported a net loss of $8.22 billion. A whopping $8.32 billion in unrealized Bitcoin losses drove that result, reflecting a decline in value that hit overall earnings. The company’s earnings per share (EPS) fell to -$24.45, missing expectations of $3.07, while revenue was $122.4 million.

These losses stem from fair value accounting, which requires companies to adjust asset values to reflect current market prices at the end of each quarter. Bitcoin closed on June 30 at $58,524 but climbed to $83,556 by September 30, marking a 42.8% increase during the quarter.

Strategy has continued to acquire Bitcoin , as its October 19 filing showed it purchased 267 BTC, valued at around $22.1 million, between October 12 and 18 at an average price of $82,900. This brings its total Bitcoin holdings to 848,517 BTC , which were purchased at a total cost of $64.02 billion, averaging $75,446 per coin.
As of October 23, MSTR shares were priced at $146, down 10% over the month but up 6.7% over the past week.
Analysts are hopeful for a return to profitability in Q3, with consensus estimates projecting earnings of $17.98 per share, compared to $8.42 during the same period last year.
Analysts’ EPS estimates for Q3 vary widely, ranging from -$0.99 to $52.82, reflecting different assumptions about Bitcoin’s quarter-end price.

The potential unrealized gain from Bitcoin will be a key focus. With Bitcoin closing at $83,556 on September 30, prices were above Strategy’s average acquisition cost of $75,446, suggesting the company may report Q3 gains. By the end of Q2, the market value of their Bitcoin holdings was $49.7 billion, compared to a $63.9 billion cost basis.

Another key topic is the company’s preferred stock, STRC. This type of stock takes priority over common shares for dividends. The recent filing reported $193.1 million in STRC buybacks and an increased buyback authorization of $3 billion, with $1.16 billion remaining. In July, CEO Phong Le noted that buying STRC shares below par would reduce future dividend obligations.

Shareholders will also vote on October 28 on paying STRC dividends daily rather than twice a month, at the current annual rate of 12%. If approved, these daily dividends could start on November 1, allowing stockholders to earn dividends for each day they own shares without worrying about specific record dates. This change could help stabilize the price fluctuations that STRC typically experiences around ex-dividend dates.

Michael Saylor stirred interest on October 23 with a post stating, “Just resolving a few Bitcoin matters behind closed doors.” Investors will likely seek clarification on this comment, as well as updates on other revenue streams, such as subscription revenue, which rose 54% in Q2 to $62.9 million. Additionally, concerns are growing regarding Strategy’s potential removal from MSCI indexes .

Yes, Strategy could report a substantial unrealized gain for Q3, given Bitcoin’s rising value, which ended the quarter 42.8% higher than where it started. However, Bitcoin’s price has dipped since September 30, trading just above $80,000, marking a 3.9% decline over the past month.

This recent decrease affects only Q4, as Q3 ended on September 30. If Bitcoin remains below its September 30 close of $83,556 through December 31, Strategy could lose some of its Q3 gains in its next quarterly report.

The company is expected to announce its Q3 earnings on October 29, 2026, though it has not yet been officially confirmed. The big question now is whether Strategy can turn that significant loss into a third-quarter profit.

In its second-quarter report released on July 30, Strategy reported a net loss of $8.22 billion. A whopping $8.32 billion in unrealized Bitcoin losses drove that result, reflecting a decline in value that hit overall earnings. The company’s earnings per share (EPS) fell to -$24.45, missing expectations of $3.07, while revenue was $122.4 million.

These losses stem from fair value accounting, which requires companies to adjust asset values to reflect current market prices at the end of each quarter. Bitcoin closed on June 30 at $58,524 but climbed to $83,556 by September 30, marking a 42.8% increase during the quarter.

Strategy has continued to acquire Bitcoin , as its October 19 filing showed it purchased 267 BTC, valued at around $22.1 million, between October 12 and 18 at an average price of $82,900. This brings its total Bitcoin holdings to 848,517 BTC , which were purchased at a total cost of $64.02 billion, averaging $75,446 per coin.
As of October 23, MSTR shares were priced at $146, down 10% over the month but up 6.7% over the past week.
Analysts are hopeful for a return to profitability in Q3, with consensus estimates projecting earnings of $17.98 per share, compared to $8.42 during the same period last year.
Analysts’ EPS estimates for Q3 vary widely, ranging from -$0.99 to $52.82, reflecting different assumptions about Bitcoin’s quarter-end price.

The potential unrealized gain from Bitcoin will be a key focus. With Bitcoin closing at $83,556 on September 30, prices were above Strategy’s average acquisition cost of $75,446, suggesting the company may report Q3 gains. By the end of Q2, the market value of their Bitcoin holdings was $49.7 billion, compared to a $63.9 billion cost basis.

Another key topic is the company’s preferred stock, STRC. This type of stock takes priority over common shares for dividends. The recent filing reported $193.1 million in STRC buybacks and an increased buyback authorization of $3 billion, with $1.16 billion remaining. In July, CEO Phong Le noted that buying STRC shares below par would reduce future dividend obligations.

Shareholders will also vote on October 28 on paying STRC dividends daily rather than twice a month, at the current annual rate of 12%. If approved, these daily dividends could start on November 1, allowing stockholders to earn dividends for each day they own shares without worrying about specific record dates. This change could help stabilize the price fluctuations that STRC typically experiences around ex-dividend dates.

Michael Saylor stirred interest on October 23 with a post stating, “Just resolving a few Bitcoin matters behind closed doors.” Investors will likely seek clarification on this comment, as well as updates on other revenue streams, such as subscription revenue, which rose 54% in Q2 to $62.9 million. Additionally, concerns are growing regarding Strategy’s potential removal from MSCI indexes .

Yes, Strategy could report a substantial unrealized gain for Q3, given Bitcoin’s rising value, which ended the quarter 42.8% higher than where it started. However, Bitcoin’s price has dipped since September 30, trading just above $80,000, marking a 3.9% decline over the past month.

This recent decrease affects only Q4, as Q3 ended on September 30. If Bitcoin remains below its September 30 close of $83,556 through December 31, Strategy could lose some of its Q3 gains in its next quarterly report.

This decline followed a sharper drop the day before, when Bitcoin sank to $79,220 on Binance, marking weekly lows at $79,107, its weakest point in over a month.

While this drop may seem limited, Bitcoin is down 3.3% for October but still up 26.8% over the last 90 days; the $80,000 threshold matters to its largest holders. Bitcoin last traded at or below $77,600 on September 18, so what caused this dip, and how much further could it fall?

External factors largely drove the downturn. Reports on October 24 indicated that the U.S. was rapidly evacuating personnel from embassies and military bases across the Middle East, citing intelligence about potential attacks by Iran on Americans. Additionally, comments from the President at a Florida rally on October 23 hinted that tensions with Iran might escalate again after the midterms.

As stock and bond markets close on weekends, investors often sell cryptocurrency to reduce risk, and Bitcoin is typically the most liquid option. Concerns about rising oil prices—West Texas Intermediate crude reached $107.89 a barrel on October 20, a spike of 13.1% in just a week—fueled inflation worries.

Further compounding the situation, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw a staggering net outflow of $635.5 million on October 22, the largest daily outflow since June, erasing the $528.4 million influx from the day before.

Interest rates don't seem to be the primary driver of this drop. On October 22, the 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.96% from 5.31% earlier in the month, and lower yields usually support Bitcoin. Meanwhile, the VIX, a measure of expected stock market volatility, rose from 14.84 to 19.03, indicating growing apprehension among stock investors.

Leveraged traders could deepen the current downturn. Coinbase ( NASDAQ: COIN ) noted that the largest cluster of net long Bitcoin positions—trades made with borrowed money that profit from rising prices—averaged at $81,993, with 64% of their dollar value entered at prices above where Bitcoin currently trades.

Liquidation occurs when an exchange must forcibly close a borrowed position because significant losses consume the trader's collateral. Each liquidation triggers a market sale that can drive further price drops, creating a chain reaction that continues until all over-leveraged positions are cleared. This type of selling often happens quickly and doesn't necessarily reflect real demand.
Currently, Bitcoin is trading below both its 50-day average of $81,798 and its 20-day average of $82,539, suggesting that many recent buyers are now at a loss, giving short-term sellers an advantage.

Cost basis, or the average price paid by a group of investors, is crucial here. According to Glassnode data, the cost basis for spot ETF holders and treasury companies—public firms holding Bitcoin on their balance sheets—falls between $80,000 and $81,500. A decline below $80,000 could push this group, including ETF buyers who put $6.3 billion into ETFs in Q3 alone, into paper losses.

Glassnode warned in its October 14 report that the largest buy orders on Binance were clustered around $80,000. A close below this ETF cost basis could eliminate the nearest support identified in Bitcoin's on-chain data. However, the dip occurred on relatively low trading volume compared to the October 24 selloff and quickly reversed, indicating a lack of strong conviction.
Bitcoin has dropped just 3.9%, while Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) has fallen 12.5% and Solana (CRYPTO: SOL) has lost 16.1%.

This resilience may stem from Bitcoin's broader base of long-term buyers, as ETFs and treasury companies hold significant amounts near their cost basis and have an incentive to defend it. In contrast, Ethereum and Solana operate in smaller markets where leveraged trading plays a larger role, and investors tend to sell riskier assets first during periods of uncertainty.

If Bitcoin cannot reclaim $81,500, $77,600 appears to be the next significant level to watch. This target aligns with Glassnode's True Market Mean—the average price paid by active investors, excluding coins that have remained inactive for years—and sits about 3.3% below the current price. ETF buyers previously positioned to defend the $80,000 floor turned sellers on October 22, while long positions near $81,993 add to the strain.
The outcome hinges on investor sentiment and external factors affecting the market.

Correlation measures how closely two assets move together based on their daily returns—the percentage change from one day's closing price to the next. A correlation of 1 means the two assets rise and fall together, while a value near zero indicates no significant relationship. Correlation primarily tracks directional movements rather than the magnitude of price changes. So, if XRP fell only half as much as Bitcoin on certain days, it could still show a high correlation because both assets move together. Traders monitor these correlations as a falling number can signal that two assets are starting to diverge. Unfortunately for XRP, the data shows it moved closer to Bitcoin in the week ending. Its relative stability was more about not falling as much during the same downtrend than about establishing any clear independence. While XRP's minimal weekly change seems promising, its performance over the last month tells a different story. Over the past 30 days, XRP has dropped 18.8%, compared with Bitcoin's relatively mild 5% decline. Year-to-date, XRP is down 29.1%, while Bitcoin is down just 7.7%. Over the past year, XRP has lost 49.8%, while Bitcoin has decreased by 27.7%. This pattern suggests XRP tends to follow Bitcoin, but often more sharply, suffering more during price drops. A flat performance after a month of steep losses could suggest easing selling pressure. However, it could also signal declining trading activity. For example, spot XRP ETFs traded only $18.8 million on October 23, down from over $102 million on October 2. The only sign of a potential break came in the 24 hours leading up to October 25, when XRP rose 1.4% while Bitcoin fell 0.4%. Yet, such a single-day movement does little to affect the broader 30-day correlation. One key factor that could push XRP away from Bitcoin is the flow of funds into spot XRP ETFs, which directly hold XRP. From October 19 to October 23, these funds saw a net inflow of about $4.3 million, including significant inflows of around $709,000 on October 21 and $3.5 million on October 22. However, these ETFs' net assets shrank from $1.77 billion on September 25 to $1.48 billion on October 23, indicating that price declines outweighed the inflows. A few million dollars per day is clearly insufficient to steer XRP away from Bitcoin's influence. Additionally, the upcoming Ripple Swell conference from October 27 to 29 in New York, combined with XRPL Apex, Ripple's developer conference, could matter. While past conferences haven't led to long-lasting rallies for XRP, any agreements related to payments or tokenized assets on the XRP Ledger could generate demand independent of Bitcoin. Short selling also presents another possibility. Reports indicated a rise in XRP margin shorts on Bitfinex, increasing from approximately 148,850 to around 300,000 in under two weeks. While these figures are unconfirmed, if XRP begins to rise, short sellers may be forced to buy back coins, creating a short squeeze that drives up demand for XRP. In conclusion, XRP has not broken away from Bitcoin. During the week ending October 25, it fell less than Bitcoin while still closely tracking its movements, resulting in a correlation of 0.97. This relationship shows that XRP continues to follow Bitcoin's lead rather than forge its own path. One week is too short to suggest separation, especially given a month in which XRP plummeted 18.8% while Bitcoin lost only 5%. However, two potential shifts could change this narrative. First, spot XRP ETFs need consistent daily inflows near the $22.6 million they saw on September 25, rather than days with no inflow, as seen in October. Additionally, XRP must close above its 50-day average around $1.41 on days when Bitcoin declines, as this would strengthen its potential to break free from Bitcoin's grasp. XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ) fell just 0.1%, making it one of the most stable major cryptocurrencies. By comparison, Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) fell 2%, Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ) fell 3.4%, and Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ) fell 2.8%. With XRP at $1.30 and Bitcoin near $80,268, some XRP holders speculate the token may be starting to decouple from Bitcoin.

Despite its flat performance over the week, the XRP-Bitcoin correlation suggests otherwise. In fact, XRP’s daily returns over the past seven days showed a strong correlation of 0.97 with Bitcoin’s movements, indicating they moved almost identically during this period. Over longer periods, the correlation remains strong: 0.91 over 30 days, 0.89 over 90 days, and 0.85 historically.

This suggests that while XRP appeared stable over the week, it has closely followed Bitcoin’s trends rather than showing separation. Is the perceived independence real, or is XRP simply falling less than Bitcoin?

Correlation measures how closely two assets move together based on their daily returns—the percentage change from one day’s closing price to the next. A correlation of 1 means the two assets rise and fall together, while a value near zero indicates no significant relationship.

Correlation primarily tracks directional movements rather than the magnitude of price changes. So, if XRP fell only half as much as Bitcoin on certain days, it could still show a high correlation because both assets move together.

Traders monitor these correlations as a falling number can signal that two assets are starting to diverge. Unfortunately for XRP, the data shows it moved closer to Bitcoin in the week ending. Its relative stability was more about not falling as much during the same downtrend than about establishing any clear independence.

While XRP’s minimal weekly change seems promising, its performance over the last month tells a different story. Over the past 30 days, XRP has dropped 18.8%, compared with Bitcoin’s relatively mild 5% decline. Year-to-date, XRP is down 29.1%, while Bitcoin is down just 7.7%.
Over the past year, XRP has lost 49.8%, while Bitcoin has decreased by 27.7%. This pattern suggests XRP tends to follow Bitcoin, but often more sharply, suffering more during price drops.

A flat performance after a month of steep losses could suggest easing selling pressure. However, it could also signal declining trading activity. For example, spot XRP ETFs traded only $18.8 million on October 23, down from over $102 million on October 2.

The only sign of a potential break came in the 24 hours leading up to October 25, when XRP rose 1.4% while Bitcoin fell 0.4%. Yet, such a single-day movement does little to affect the broader 30-day correlation.

One key factor that could push XRP away from Bitcoin is the flow of funds into spot XRP ETFs, which directly hold XRP. From October 19 to October 23, these funds saw a net inflow of about $4.3 million, including significant inflows of around $709,000 on October 21 and $3.5 million on October 22.

However, these ETFs’ net assets shrank from $1.77 billion on September 25 to $1.48 billion on October 23, indicating that price declines outweighed the inflows. A few million dollars per day is clearly insufficient to steer XRP away from Bitcoin’s influence.

Additionally, the upcoming Ripple Swell conference from October 27 to 29 in New York, combined with XRPL Apex, Ripple’s developer conference, could matter. While past conferences haven’t led to long-lasting rallies for XRP, any agreements related to payments or tokenized assets on the XRP Ledger could generate demand independent of Bitcoin.

Short selling also presents another possibility. Reports indicated a rise in XRP margin shorts on Bitfinex, increasing from approximately 148,850 to around 300,000 in under two weeks. While these figures are unconfirmed, if XRP begins to rise, short sellers may be forced to buy back coins, creating a short squeeze that drives up demand for XRP.

In conclusion, XRP has not broken away from Bitcoin. During the week ending October 25, it fell less than Bitcoin while still closely tracking its movements, resulting in a correlation of 0.97. This relationship shows that XRP continues to follow Bitcoin’s lead rather than forge its own path. One week is too short to suggest separation, especially given a month in which XRP plummeted 18.8% while Bitcoin lost only 5%.

However, two potential shifts could change this narrative. First, spot XRP ETFs need consistent daily inflows near the $22.6 million they saw on September 25, rather than days with no inflow, as seen in October. Additionally, XRP must close above its 50-day average around $1.41 on days when Bitcoin declines, as this would strengthen its potential to break free from Bitcoin’s grasp.

Hence, fewer buyers are coming in from this zone, meaning ETH could quickly decline if it breaks below the August 20 low.

As of now, the Ethereum Foundation has not set a new date for the Hoodi upgrade or confirmed when it will reach the main network. Historically, past upgrades have not significantly boosted prices.

extraction.body: Your Mac comes with a fairly robust suite of built-in privacy tools. If you think about it too hard, you'll start sweating at the reality of how much personal data you have on your MacBook . Whether it's sensitive documents or credentials and logins, you'd probably like to keep all of it secure. And while Apple has built its brand around being particularly privacy- and security-focused, that doesn't mean you shouldn't take the time to go through your settings and make sure your MacBook is as safe as it can be. After all, something like hopping on an unsecured public Wi-Fi network could leave you vulnerable, and not everyone has the best habits when it comes to protections like passwords. Your individual privacy and security needs will vary depending on who you are, what you do and how you do it. While this list isn't exhaustive, it's a place to start. So, if it's been a while, or perhaps you've just bought a new MacBook, it might be time to take a spin through your privacy settings. From location services to your lock screen password, here are some areas you should double-check. This is especially important if you don't always have eyes on your MacBook. You can require a password to wake your laptop up from sleep or your screensaver. You also have the option to decide how long your laptop must be asleep before prompting. To tweak these settings, go to System Settings > Lock Screen . Another setting to revisit is Location Services. Location Services is what lets apps, websites or the like get information about where you are. In cases like Google or Apple Maps, it can be useful and even necessary for the app to work. It's worth considering, though, that not every app that's accessing your location needs to. If you go to Settings, then Privacy & Security, you'll find Location Services. There you can either wholesale turn everything off, or individually grant or revoke apps' access to your location. Similarly, you can decide which apps have access to your camera and microphone by checking those individual settings under Privacy & Security and toggling your choices on or off. Odds are, when you're on your MacBook, you're likely also on a Wi-Fi network . You can actually decide how your MacBook joins those Wi-Fi networks. If you go to Settings > Wi-Fi, make sure your computer doesn't automatically join unsecured Wi-Fi networks, which could open you up to malware or data interception . One of the settings options will send you a notification asking for permission before joining anything. That way, you can stay in control. sources.title: Nvidia discusses $2,000-per-GPU annual fee for software that 'runs agents on AI factories' — details unclear about potential overlaps, firm already charges more than twice that amount for its AI Enterprise software platform - Tom's Hardware
passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has put the annual cost of licensing the company’s AI software at around $2,000 per GPU to 'run all the software that Nvidia provides that runs agents on these AI factories,' according to a recent video of the comments (below), a pricing model that could generate $50 billion over five years under a proposed scenario involving five million paid licenses outlined by FourWeekMBA .
It’s also unclear which software the license would cover, or if there is overlap between products.
The distinction matters because Nvidia already charges for enterprise software.
Its AI Enterprise platform is listed at $4,500 per GPU for a one-year subscription.
It should not be treated as a confirmed price cut.
Enterprises deploying AI agents need security, governance and someone accountable for keeping the stack running.
My bet: OpenShell becomes the standard security layer for enterprise AI, driving adoption of NVIDIA’s paid software and support.
Each new year of GPU sales adds another potential stream of software revenue.
Nvidia had previously introduced its Open Agent Safety Platform in September.
The newer reference architecture builds on that effort, extending the approach to enterprise infrastructure and edge systems.
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.
The licensing discussion comes as Nvidia develops more of the infrastructure needed to deploy and manage AI agents in enterprise environments.
These systems can use tools, access data, and execute tasks, creating new security and management challenges for businesses running them at scale.

On October 21, Nvidia announced its OpenShell Reference Architecture , a system that combines its Vera Rubin computing infrastructure, Vera CPUs, and BlueField-4 data processing units (DPUs) running Nvidia Sentry.
OpenShell provides a secure runtime for AI agents , establishing boundaries around their actions and access to tools and resources.
Sentry monitors agent activity independently and can quarantine an agent that attempts to cross those boundaries, according to Nvidia.
The architecture is designed to bring security controls into the underlying infrastructure rather than relying solely on safeguards built into an AI model or application.

Nvidia’s reported $2,000 annual fee per GPU could turn its software business into a multibillion-dollar revenue stream, but Huang has yet to reveal when the pricing could take effect. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has put the annual cost of licensing the company’s AI software at around $2,000 per GPU to 'run all the software that Nvidia provides that runs agents on these AI factories,' according to a recent video of the comments (below), a pricing model that could generate $50 billion over five years under a proposed scenario involving five million paid licenses outlined by FourWeekMBA . Huang discussed the pricing at GTC Berlin on October 22, where the company outlined its broader push to build an AI infrastructure business spanning chips, software and AI-agent security . “Software licensing will become increasingly a major part of our company’s business. The way that we license will be…for example, it’s about $2,000 per GPU per year to run all the software that Nvidia provides that runs agents on these AI factories,” said Huang. The numbers add up quickly. At $2,000 per GPU each year, Nvidia would bring in $10 billion annually if five million GPUs were covered by paid licenses. Over five years, that would amount to $50 billion, provided customers kept renewing their subscriptions. The catch, however, is that Nvidia has not disclosed how many GPUs could be covered by the proposed $2,000 fee, or whether that’s its standard price. It’s also unclear which software the license would cover, or if there is overlap between products. The distinction matters because Nvidia already charges for enterprise software. Its AI Enterprise platform is listed at $4,500 per GPU for a one-year subscription. Huang’s reported $2,000 figure is lower, but Nvidia has not confirmed that the two prices cover the same products or licensing terms. It should not be treated as a confirmed price cut. Jensen’s ~$2,000 per GPU per year in enterprise software deserves more attention. Enterprises deploying AI agents need security, governance and someone accountable for keeping the stack running. My bet: OpenShell becomes the standard security layer for enterprise AI, driving adoption of NVIDIA’s paid software and support. Consider the math. Assume: • 10M eligible enterprise GPUs shipped in a year • 50% paid software attach • $2,000 per GPU annually That’s $10B in annual recurring revenue potential. Keep those subscriptions for five years and you get $50B from a single year’s GPU shipments. Each new year of GPU sales adds another potential stream of software revenue. $NVDA October 22, 2026 The licensing discussion comes as Nvidia develops more of the infrastructure needed to deploy and manage AI agents in enterprise environments. These systems can use tools, access data, and execute tasks, creating new security and management challenges for businesses running them at scale. On October 21, Nvidia announced its OpenShell Reference Architecture , a system that combines its Vera Rubin computing infrastructure, Vera CPUs, and BlueField-4 data processing units (DPUs) running Nvidia Sentry. OpenShell provides a secure runtime for AI agents , establishing boundaries around their actions and access to tools and resources. Sentry monitors agent activity independently and can quarantine an agent that attempts to cross those boundaries, according to Nvidia. The architecture is designed to bring security controls into the underlying infrastructure rather than relying solely on safeguards built into an AI model or application. Nvidia had previously introduced its Open Agent Safety Platform in September. The newer reference architecture builds on that effort, extending the approach to enterprise infrastructure and edge systems. Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox. Other companies are also incorporating these controls into their products. Anthropic is integrating OpenShell and BlueField hardware with Claude Managed Agents to give businesses additional control over what their AI agents can access inside execution sandboxes. Salesforce has developed a Slack Admin Bridge for OpenShell that lets administrators review agent access requests, approve or reject permissions, and monitor activity directly in Slack. The proposed software pricing fits Huang’s wider argument that Nvidia is becoming more than a supplier of GPUs. The company has expanded into networking, systems, enterprise software, and infrastructure designed to run AI workloads. Speaking on the BG2Pod podcast recently, Huang said, “One of these days, people might not categorize us as a chip company anymore.” He pointed to Nvidia’s presence across industries including healthcare, automotive, telecommunications and life sciences, where the company provides broader technology stacks rather than chips alone. That said, Nvidia has not said when the $2,000-per-GPU fee would take effect or which software it would cover. It also remains unclear how the proposed pricing would fit into the company’s existing enterprise software business. Sentry monitors agent activity independently and can quarantine an agent that attempts to cross those boundaries, according to Nvidia. The architecture is designed to bring security controls into the underlying infrastructure rather than relying solely on safeguards built into an AI model or application.

Nvidia had previously introduced its Open Agent Safety Platform in September. The newer reference architecture builds on that effort, extending the approach to enterprise infrastructure and edge systems.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Other companies are also incorporating these controls into their products. Anthropic is integrating OpenShell and BlueField hardware with Claude Managed Agents to give businesses additional control over what their AI agents can access inside execution sandboxes. Salesforce has developed a Slack Admin Bridge for OpenShell that lets administrators review agent access requests, approve or reject permissions, and monitor activity directly in Slack.

The proposed software pricing fits Huang’s wider argument that Nvidia is becoming more than a supplier of GPUs. The company has expanded into networking, systems, enterprise software, and infrastructure designed to run AI workloads. Speaking on the BG2Pod podcast recently, Huang said, “One of these days, people might not categorize us as a chip company anymore.” He pointed to Nvidia’s presence across industries including healthcare, automotive, telecommunications and life sciences, where the company provides broader technology stacks rather than chips alone.

That said, Nvidia has not said when the $2,000-per-GPU fee would take effect or which software it would cover. It also remains unclear how the proposed pricing would fit into the company’s existing enterprise software business.

story.title: Nvidia discusses $2,000-per-GPU annual fee for software that 'runs agents on AI factories' — details unclear about potential overlaps, firm already charges more than twice that amount for its AI Enterprise software platform - Tom's Hardware

facts.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has put the annual cost of licensing the company’s AI software at around $2,000 per GPU to 'run all the software that Nvidia provides that runs agents on these AI factories,' according to a recent video of the comments (below), a pricing model that could generate $50 billion over five years under a proposed scenario involving five million paid licenses outlined by FourWeekMBA .
It’s also unclear which software the license would cover, or if there is overlap between products.
The distinction matters because Nvidia already charges for enterprise software.
Its AI Enterprise platform is listed at $4,500 per GPU for a one-year subscription.
It should not be treated as a confirmed price cut.
Enterprises deploying AI agents need security, governance and someone accountable for keeping the stack running.
My bet: OpenShell becomes the standard security layer for enterprise AI, driving adoption of NVIDIA’s paid software and support.
Each new year of GPU sales adds another potential stream of software revenue.
Nvidia had previously introduced its Open Agent Safety Platform in September.
The newer reference architecture builds on that effort, extending the approach to enterprise infrastructure and edge systems.
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.
The licensing discussion comes as Nvidia develops more of the infrastructure needed to deploy and manage AI agents in enterprise environments.
These systems can use tools, access data, and execute tasks, creating new security and management challenges for businesses running them at scale.

On October 21, Nvidia announced its OpenShell Reference Architecture , a system that combines its Vera Rubin computing infrastructure, Vera CPUs, and BlueField-4 data processing units (DPUs) running Nvidia Sentry.
OpenShell provides a secure runtime for AI agents , establishing boundaries around their actions and access to tools and resources.
Sentry monitors agent activity independently and can quarantine an agent that attempts to cross those boundaries, according to Nvidia.
The architecture is designed to bring security controls into the underlying infrastructure rather than relying solely on safeguards built into an AI model or application.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has put the annual cost of licensing the company’s AI software at around $2,000 per GPU to 'run all the software that Nvidia provides that runs agents on these AI factories,' according to a recent video of the comments (below), a pricing model that could generate $50 billion over five years under a proposed scenario involving five million paid licenses outlined by FourWeekMBA . Huang discussed the pricing at GTC Berlin on October 22, where the company outlined its broader push to build an AI infrastructure business spanning chips, software and AI-agent security . “Software licensing will become increasingly a major part of our company’s business. The way that we license will be…for example, it’s about $2,000 per GPU per year to run all the software that Nvidia provides that runs agents on these AI factories,” said Huang. The numbers add up quickly. At $2,000 per GPU each year, Nvidia would bring in $10 billion annually if five million GPUs were covered by paid licenses. Over five years, that would amount to $50 billion, provided customers kept renewing their subscriptions. The catch, however, is that Nvidia has not disclosed how many GPUs could be covered by the proposed $2,000 fee, or whether that’s its standard price. It’s also unclear which software the license would cover, or if there is overlap between products. The distinction matters because Nvidia already charges for enterprise software. Its AI Enterprise platform is listed at $4,500 per GPU for a one-year subscription. Huang’s reported $2,000 figure is lower, but Nvidia has not confirmed that the two prices cover the same products or licensing terms. It should not be treated as a confirmed price cut. Jensen’s ~$2,000 per GPU per year in enterprise software deserves more attention. Enterprises deploying AI agents need security, governance and someone accountable for keeping the stack running. My bet: OpenShell becomes the standard security layer for enterprise AI, driving adoption of NVIDIA’s paid software and support. Consider the math. Assume: • 10M eligible enterprise GPUs shipped in a year • 50% paid software attach • $2,000 per GPU annually That’s $10B in annual recurring revenue potential. Keep those subscriptions for five years and you get $50B from a single year’s GPU shipments. Each new year of GPU sales adds another potential stream of software revenue. $NVDA October 22, 2026 The licensing discussion comes as Nvidia develops more of the infrastructure needed to deploy and manage AI agents in enterprise environments. These systems can use tools, access data, and execute tasks, creating new security and management challenges for businesses running them at scale. On October 21, Nvidia announced its OpenShell Reference Architecture , a system that combines its Vera Rubin computing infrastructure, Vera CPUs, and BlueField-4 data processing units (DPUs) running Nvidia Sentry. OpenShell provides a secure runtime for AI agents , establishing boundaries around their actions and access to tools and resources. Sentry monitors agent activity independently and can quarantine an agent that attempts to cross those boundaries, according to Nvidia. The architecture is designed to bring security controls into the underlying infrastructure rather than relying solely on safeguards built into an AI model or application. Nvidia had previously introduced its Open Agent Safety Platform in September. The newer reference architecture builds on that effort, extending the approach to enterprise infrastructure and edge systems. Anthropic is integrating OpenShell and BlueField hardware with Claude Managed Agents to give businesses additional control over what their AI agents can access inside execution sandboxes. Salesforce has developed a Slack Admin Bridge for OpenShell that lets administrators review agent access requests, approve or reject permissions, and monitor activity directly in Slack. The proposed software pricing fits Huang’s wider argument that Nvidia is becoming more than a supplier of GPUs. The company has expanded into networking, systems, enterprise software, and infrastructure designed to run AI workloads. Speaking on the BG2Pod podcast recently, Huang said, “One of these days, people might not categorize us as a chip company anymore.” He pointed to Nvidia’s presence across industries including healthcare, automotive, telecommunications and life sciences, where the company provides broader technology stacks rather than chips alone. That said, Nvidia has not said when the $2,000-per-GPU fee would take effect or which software it would cover. It also remains unclear how the proposed pricing would fit into the company’s existing enterprise software business. Nvidia’s reported $2,000 annual fee per GPU could turn its software business into a multibillion-dollar revenue stream, but Huang has yet to reveal when the pricing could take effect.
When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works .

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has put the annual cost of licensing the company’s AI software at around $2,000 per GPU to 'run all the software that Nvidia provides that runs agents on these AI factories,' according to a recent video of the comments (below), a pricing model that could generate $50 billion over five years under a proposed scenario involving five million paid licenses outlined by FourWeekMBA .

Huang discussed the pricing at GTC Berlin on October 22, where the company outlined its broader push to build an AI infrastructure business spanning chips, software and AI-agent security . “Software licensing will become increasingly a major part of our company’s business. The way that we license will be…for example, it’s about $2,000 per GPU per year to run all the software that Nvidia provides that runs agents on these AI factories,” said Huang.

The numbers add up quickly. At $2,000 per GPU each year, Nvidia would bring in $10 billion annually if five million GPUs were covered by paid licenses. Over five years, that would amount to $50 billion, provided customers kept renewing their subscriptions. The catch, however, is that Nvidia has not disclosed how many GPUs could be covered by the proposed $2,000 fee, or whether that’s its standard price. It’s also unclear which software the license would cover, or if there is overlap between products.

The distinction matters because Nvidia already charges for enterprise software. Its AI Enterprise platform is listed at $4,500 per GPU for a one-year subscription. Huang’s reported $2,000 figure is lower, but Nvidia has not confirmed that the two prices cover the same products or licensing terms. It should not be treated as a confirmed price cut.

Jensen’s ~$2,000 per GPU per year in enterprise software deserves more attention. Enterprises deploying AI agents need security, governance and someone accountable for keeping the stack running. My bet: OpenShell becomes the standard security layer for enterprise AI, driving adoption of NVIDIA’s paid software and support. Consider the math. Assume: • 10M eligible enterprise GPUs shipped in a year • 50% paid software attach • $2,000 per GPU annually That’s $10B in annual recurring revenue potential. Keep those subscriptions for five years and you get $50B from a single year’s GPU shipments. Each new year of GPU sales adds another potential stream of software revenue. $NVDA October 22, 2026

The licensing discussion comes as Nvidia develops more of the infrastructure needed to deploy and manage AI agents in enterprise environments. These systems can use tools, access data, and execute tasks, creating new security and management challenges for businesses running them at scale.

On October 21, Nvidia announced its OpenShell Reference Architecture , a system that combines its Vera Rubin computing infrastructure, Vera CPUs, and BlueField-4 data processing units (DPUs) running Nvidia Sentry. OpenShell provides a secure runtime for AI agents , establishing boundaries around their actions and access to tools and resources. Sentry monitors agent activity independently and can quarantine an agent that attempts to cross those boundaries, according to Nvidia. The architecture is designed to bring security controls into the underlying infrastructure rather than relying solely on safeguards built into an AI model or application.

Nvidia had previously introduced its Open Agent Safety Platform in September. The newer reference architecture builds on that effort, extending the approach to enterprise infrastructure and edge systems.

Other companies are also incorporating these controls into their products. Anthropic is integrating OpenShell and BlueField hardware with Claude Managed Agents to give businesses additional control over what their AI agents can access inside execution sandboxes. Salesforce has developed a Slack Admin Bridge for OpenShell that lets administrators review agent access requests, approve or reject permissions, and monitor activity directly in Slack.

The proposed software pricing fits Huang’s wider argument that Nvidia is becoming more than a supplier of GPUs. The company has expanded into networking, systems, enterprise software, and infrastructure designed to run AI workloads. Speaking on the BG2Pod podcast recently, Huang said, “One of these days, people might not categorize us as a chip company anymore.” He pointed to Nvidia’s presence across industries including healthcare, automotive, telecommunications and life sciences, where the company provides broader technology stacks rather than chips alone.

That said, Nvidia has not said when the $2,000-per-GPU fee would take effect or which software it would cover. It also remains unclear how the proposed pricing would fit into the company’s existing enterprise software business.

extraction.body: A slew of AI-powered gadgets on the market aims to integrate artificial intelligence into our daily lives like never before. Some of these AI wearables — including necklaces, rings, and wristbands, as well as portable devices — serve as productivity tools, while others claim to act as friendly companions listening to your everyday thoughts. Even OpenAI is working on a compact AI companion device. Below, we’ve rounded up some of the most notable devices. The companion app (currently available only on iOS) is included with a $19 monthly subscription. The app allows you to interact with Bee directly and ask it questions. You can also get key takeaways from your day and chronological transcripts of your conversations. Amazon acquired the wearables startup in July 2025, launching its first new products earlier this month. Amazon introduced two new devices: the Bee Frontier, priced at $74.99, which can be worn on the wrist or clipped to clothing, and the Bee Eclipse, priced at $99.99, a credit-card-sized device that attaches magnetically to the back of a smartphone. This $129 white pendant hangs around your neck and functions as an emotional support companion. It recognizes your tone and mood, allowing you to chat with it as if it were a friend. It connects to your phone via Bluetooth and constantly listens, ready to respond or send you proactive messages, like wishing you good luck before an interview. However, it has also faced criticism, including backlash against its subway ad campaign in NYC. People vandalized the ads, writing messages like “surveillance capitalism.” Likely as an attempt to stay relevant, the company recently unveiled a major product update, introducing a new voice feature. Under the name “Friend 2.0,” the updated device includes a built-in speaker that allows it to communicate with users and express a more distinctive personality. Formerly known as Rewind, Limitless is another conversation-recording pendant priced at $99. Nirva plans to open orders in November, with shipments to early users targeted for the end of the year. The device will cost $249. Priced at $89, this device can answer your questions, summarize your conversations, create to-do lists, and help schedule meetings. Additionally, Omi is constantly listening and running your conversations through ChatGPT, allowing it to remember the context about you and offer personalized advice. Omi can be worn as a necklace, but another notable aspect is that it can be attached to the side of your head with medical tape and can detect when you’re speaking to it. The tiny wearable voice recorder can be worn on your wrist or attached magnetically to your clothing. The recordings are saved in real time on your phone, eliminating the hassle of manual note-taking. The device includes 300 free monthly transcription minutes, but with the $8.33 per month Pro plan, you upgrade your transcription time to 1,200 minutes. This year, the company is gearing up to launch a $179 ultra-thin note-taking device called the Plaud Note Pro , which is now available for preorder. Rabbit R1 is another AI gadget that has quickly become a topic of interest in the tech world, despite facing some challenges during its initial launch. This small, retro-styled handheld device features a touchscreen and rotating camera, at a price point of $199.

sources.title: 4 Ray-Ban Meta Privacy Settings You Should Change Before Wearing Them - Engadget
passages: Add microphones that listen for "Hey Meta" and optional cloud storage to the mix, and now you'd want to go through the privacy menu before wearing them everywhere.
To turn it off, go to Glasses privacy > Cloud media in the settings of your glasses in the Meta AI app.
If you have more than one pair of Meta glasses, like the first-generation Ray-Ban Meta glasses , you will need to change this setting separately on each pair.
So, turning Cloud media off won't change how Meta processes visual AI requests.
sources.body: Add microphones that listen for "Hey Meta" and optional cloud storage to the mix, and now you'd want to go through the privacy menu before wearing them everywhere. To turn it off, go to Glasses privacy > Cloud media in the settings of your glasses in the Meta AI app. If you have more than one pair of Meta glasses, like the first-generation Ray-Ban Meta glasses , you will need to change this setting separately on each pair. So, turning Cloud media off won't change how Meta processes visual AI requests.

extraction.body: Meta gives you some control over what your glasses collect and store. You just have to know where to look. Ray-Ban Meta glasses can snap a photo with a tap, but it's a bit trickier to find out what happens to that photo, or anything else you send to Meta AI. Add microphones that listen for "Hey Meta" and optional cloud storage to the mix, and now you'd want to go through the privacy menu before wearing them everywhere. Gallery photos and images processed by Meta AI follow different rules, and some data sharing is optional. Here are four options you can consider to reduce the amount of data that's collected, uploaded or stored, but at the cost of some convenience. You can call on the assistant by saying "Hey Meta," which is convenient, until a normal conversation sounds enough like the wake phrase to accidentally activate it. The glasses are always listening for those two words when voice activation is turned on. There's one more reason to think twice about leaving it on. In the US, users can no longer prevent Meta from storing recordings of their AI voice interactions in the cloud. You can manually delete saved recordings, but you'll need to remember to do it. If you don't want to use voice activation, simply wear your glasses and ensure they are connected to your phone. Open the Meta AI app, choose your glasses and go to Meta AI > "Hey Meta" preferences. Deactivate the "Hey Meta" toggle. The touchpad on the right temple can still be used to call the assistant, and the microphones are still available for calls and videos. Meta will also continue processing audio when you intentionally use the assistant. Previous voice interactions can be seen or deleted under Glasses privacy > Voice activity log. Photos and videos captured for your gallery normally stay on the glasses until you import them to your phone. Enable Cloud media, however, and Meta can keep copies on its servers for up to 30 days. That's quite a detour for a picture that was just going to your camera roll. To turn it off, go to Glasses privacy > Cloud media in the settings of your glasses in the Meta AI app. You can still take photos, record videos and import them to your phone. The things you lose are cloud-based features such as voice-controlled photo sharing and autocapture. Meta says ordinary gallery captures aren't used to train its AI models or serve ads, regardless of this setting. However, there is a key difference here: Disabling Cloud media won't prevent images from being sent to Meta when you ask its assistant a visual question. The backup options on your phone are also important. If you use iCloud or Google Photos for automatic backup, those photos you import may still be backed up to the cloud, just on someone else's servers. Photos aren't the only information Meta collects from its smart glasses. The company makes a distinction between data it needs to operate the device and optional "additional data," such as usage analytics on which features you use and how often. Those details could help Meta to better understand how people use its products. Whether you want to volunteer that info is another story, particularly if the glasses are something you may wear all day. To turn off this sharing, open the Meta AI app, choose your connected glasses and then go to Glasses privacy > Share additional data and turn the toggle off. Unlike disabling the wake phrase or Cloud media, this won't change the way you engage with your photos, make calls or listen to music. It doesn't shut off all data collection, either. Meta continues to collect data it says it needs to run and ensure the safety of the glasses, and voice commands and AI requests via the camera are governed by its own guidelines. Turning off additional data sharing also won't delete information Meta has already collected. In September 2026, Meta introduced an option to stop visual data from smart glasses interactions from being used for AI training. Visual data is sent to Meta's servers to generate an answer when you ask the assistant to identify a plant or translate a menu. Previously, that information could be stored for AI training, including review by human contractors. This is separate from the photos and videos you intentionally save to your gallery. So, turning Cloud media off won't change how Meta processes visual AI requests. To opt out, open your glasses' settings in the Meta AI app, select Meta AI and disable Store visual data from AI experiences . Your glasses need to be out of the case and connected to your phone. Meta says it still has to process images to provide answers to your queries, but it will not keep that data for AI training or make it available to human reviewers for product improvement after you opt out. There are some compromises, though. Visual reminders, including requests for the glasses to remember an object for later, may no longer work. Meta hasn't specified whether other features might be affected. Plus, the setting does not clear out previously processed visual information or alter the way voice interactions are processed. If you have more than one pair of Meta glasses, like the first-generation Ray-Ban Meta glasses , you will need to change this setting separately on each pair.

AI spending is generating revenue for technology providers, but most other S&P 500 companies have yet to show comparable gains in productivity or profit margins, a report by Apollo’s Daily Spark analysis has shown. Artificial intelligence has helped fuel a boom in technology spending, but the financial benefits remain difficult to spot across much of corporate America. Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok said on October 24 that revenue per worker and profit margins were rising for the Magnificent Seven technology stocks while remaining flat across the other 493 companies in the S&P 500. Notably, Slok’s analysis found no clear evidence that AI is boosting productivity growth, despite heavy investment in the technology. Revenue per worker and profit margins have risen among the Magnificent Seven but remain flat across the other 493 companies in the S&P 500, according to the report. “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok wrote. Running AI models at scale can quickly drive up costs since many providers charge by token usage, so bills climb as employees make more requests or AI agents process data and handle increasingly complex tasks. Slok said mainstream companies were beginning to view token spending as a cost center rather than a source of growth. Venture capital-backed businesses are spending more on tokens, he noted, while established companies have less incentive to pay for the newest models if cheaper alternatives can do the job. That creates a problem for AI providers hoping to turn growing adoption into a lasting revenue stream. Selling more computing power and model access can boost suppliers’ sales, but customers need to see corresponding gains in productivity, revenue or operating costs to keep spending at the same pace. Moreover, if AI expenses rise without a measurable improvement in business performance, the additional spending could weigh on margins. “AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.” Slok added. “The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector.” Slok’s analysis also points to a broader limitation: AI adoption remains concentrated among a relatively small group of companies. Unless usage spreads across more industries and produces measurable results, the technology’s effect on the wider economy could remain limited. Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox. The same tension is emerging in India’s financial technology sector. A PwC India survey reported by Business Standard on September 11 found that 84% of surveyed fintech respondents had yet to see measurable financial results from their AI investments. That has not stopped companies from pressing ahead. The survey also found that 48% of respondents identified proprietary intelligence as a leading strategic priority. Meanwhile, 30% expected customer experience to drive AI agent adoption over the next three to five years, followed by cost reduction and productivity gains at 22%. Trust is another hurdle for businesses looking to deploy AI agents in financial services . As per the survey, 41% of respondents identified customer trust and adoption as the biggest barriers to scaling agentic payments, while 33% pointed to fraud, security and risk management as major concerns. AI agents could expand the technology’s role in business by handling multistep tasks rather than simply responding to prompts, although their ability to access tools, process information and act across company systems also brings additional usage costs and security concerns. Nvidia has been developing tools to address some of those risks, previously, introducing its Open Agent Safety Platform , a hardware-and-software security stack designed to help businesses control AI agents and restrict potentially harmful actions. Rising token consumption has also prompted companies including Microsoft , Meta and Amazon to rein in AI usage as employees adopt the tools and agentic workloads drive up bills. The trend highlights a growing challenge for businesses: encouraging wider AI adoption without allowing operating costs to spiral. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has also acknowledged the problem, describing AI token costs as a “huge issue” for customers seeking better value from their spending. The infrastructure behind the AI boom carries its own price tag with Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft having committed enormous sums to data centers, chips and the power needed to run AI workloads. AI spending is generating revenue for technology providers, but most other S&P 500 companies have yet to show comparable gains in productivity or profit margins, a report by Apollo’s Daily Spark analysis has shown.

Artificial intelligence has helped fuel a boom in technology spending, but the financial benefits remain difficult to spot across much of corporate America. Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok said on October 24 that revenue per worker and profit margins were rising for the Magnificent Seven technology stocks while remaining flat across the other 493 companies in the S&P 500.

Notably, Slok’s analysis found no clear evidence that AI is boosting productivity growth, despite heavy investment in the technology. Revenue per worker and profit margins have risen among the Magnificent Seven but remain flat across the other 493 companies in the S&P 500, according to the report. “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok wrote.

Running AI models at scale can quickly drive up costs since many providers charge by token usage, so bills climb as employees make more requests or AI agents process data and handle increasingly complex tasks. Slok said mainstream companies were beginning to view token spending as a cost center rather than a source of growth. Venture capital-backed businesses are spending more on tokens, he noted, while established companies have less incentive to pay for the newest models if cheaper alternatives can do the job.

That creates a problem for AI providers hoping to turn growing adoption into a lasting revenue stream. Selling more computing power and model access can boost suppliers’ sales, but customers need to see corresponding gains in productivity, revenue or operating costs to keep spending at the same pace. Moreover, if AI expenses rise without a measurable improvement in business performance, the additional spending could weigh on margins.

“AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.” Slok added. “The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector.”

Slok’s analysis also points to a broader limitation: AI adoption remains concentrated among a relatively small group of companies. Unless usage spreads across more industries and produces measurable results, the technology’s effect on the wider economy could remain limited.

The same tension is emerging in India’s financial technology sector. A PwC India survey reported by Business Standard on September 11 found that 84% of surveyed fintech respondents had yet to see measurable financial results from their AI investments.

That has not stopped companies from pressing ahead. The survey also found that 48% of respondents identified proprietary intelligence as a leading strategic priority. Meanwhile, 30% expected customer experience to drive AI agent adoption over the next three to five years, followed by cost reduction and productivity gains at 22%.

Trust is another hurdle for businesses looking to deploy AI agents in financial services . As per the survey, 41% of respondents identified customer trust and adoption as the biggest barriers to scaling agentic payments, while 33% pointed to fraud, security and risk management as major concerns.

AI agents could expand the technology’s role in business by handling multistep tasks rather than simply responding to prompts, although their ability to access tools, process information and act across company systems also brings additional usage costs and security concerns.

Nvidia has been developing tools to address some of those risks, previously, introducing its Open Agent Safety Platform , a hardware-and-software security stack designed to help businesses control AI agents and restrict potentially harmful actions. Rising token consumption has also prompted companies including Microsoft , Meta and Amazon to rein in AI usage as employees adopt the tools and agentic workloads drive up bills. The trend highlights a growing challenge for businesses: encouraging wider AI adoption without allowing operating costs to spiral.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has also acknowledged the problem, describing AI token costs as a “huge issue” for customers seeking better value from their spending. The infrastructure behind the AI boom carries its own price tag with Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft having committed enormous sums to data centers, chips and the power needed to run AI workloads.

AI spending is generating revenue for technology providers, but most other S&P 500 companies have yet to show comparable gains in productivity or profit margins, a report by Apollo’s Daily Spark analysis has shown. Artificial intelligence has helped fuel a boom in technology spending, but the financial benefits remain difficult to spot across much of corporate America. Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok said on October 24 that revenue per worker and profit margins were rising for the Magnificent Seven technology stocks while remaining flat across the other 493 companies in the S&P 500. Notably, Slok’s analysis found no clear evidence that AI is boosting productivity growth, despite heavy investment in the technology. Revenue per worker and profit margins have risen among the Magnificent Seven but remain flat across the other 493 companies in the S&P 500, according to the report. “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok wrote. Running AI models at scale can quickly drive up costs since many providers charge by token usage, so bills climb as employees make more requests or AI agents process data and handle increasingly complex tasks. Slok said mainstream companies were beginning to view token spending as a cost center rather than a source of growth. Venture capital-backed businesses are spending more on tokens, he noted, while established companies have less incentive to pay for the newest models if cheaper alternatives can do the job. That creates a problem for AI providers hoping to turn growing adoption into a lasting revenue stream. Selling more computing power and model access can boost suppliers’ sales, but customers need to see corresponding gains in productivity, revenue or operating costs to keep spending at the same pace. Moreover, if AI expenses rise without a measurable improvement in business performance, the additional spending could weigh on margins. “AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.” Slok added. “The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector.” Slok’s analysis also points to a broader limitation: AI adoption remains concentrated among a relatively small group of companies. Unless usage spreads across more industries and produces measurable results, the technology’s effect on the wider economy could remain limited. Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox. The same tension is emerging in India’s financial technology sector. A PwC India survey reported by Business Standard on September 11 found that 84% of surveyed fintech respondents had yet to see measurable financial results from their AI investments. That has not stopped companies from pressing ahead. The survey also found that 48% of respondents identified proprietary intelligence as a leading strategic priority. Meanwhile, 30% expected customer experience to drive AI agent adoption over the next three to five years, followed by cost reduction and productivity gains at 22%. Trust is another hurdle for businesses looking to deploy AI agents in financial services . As per the survey, 41% of respondents identified customer trust and adoption as the biggest barriers to scaling agentic payments, while 33% pointed to fraud, security and risk management as major concerns. AI agents could expand the technology’s role in business by handling multistep tasks rather than simply responding to prompts, although their ability to access tools, process information and act across company systems also brings additional usage costs and security concerns. Nvidia has been developing tools to address some of those risks, previously, introducing its Open Agent Safety Platform , a hardware-and-software security stack designed to help businesses control AI agents and restrict potentially harmful actions. Rising token consumption has also prompted companies including Microsoft , Meta and Amazon to rein in AI usage as employees adopt the tools and agentic workloads drive up bills. The trend highlights a growing challenge for businesses: encouraging wider AI adoption without allowing operating costs to spiral. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has also acknowledged the problem, describing AI token costs as a “huge issue” for customers seeking better value from their spending. The infrastructure behind the AI boom carries its own price tag with Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft having committed enormous sums to data centers, chips and the power needed to run AI workloads. AI spending is generating revenue for technology providers, but most other S&P 500 companies have yet to show comparable gains in productivity or profit margins, a report by Apollo’s Daily Spark analysis has shown.

Artificial intelligence has helped fuel a boom in technology spending, but the financial benefits remain difficult to spot across much of corporate America. Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok said on October 24 that revenue per worker and profit margins were rising for the Magnificent Seven technology stocks while remaining flat across the other 493 companies in the S&P 500.

Notably, Slok’s analysis found no clear evidence that AI is boosting productivity growth, despite heavy investment in the technology. Revenue per worker and profit margins have risen among the Magnificent Seven but remain flat across the other 493 companies in the S&P 500, according to the report. “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok wrote.

Running AI models at scale can quickly drive up costs since many providers charge by token usage, so bills climb as employees make more requests or AI agents process data and handle increasingly complex tasks. Slok said mainstream companies were beginning to view token spending as a cost center rather than a source of growth. Venture capital-backed businesses are spending more on tokens, he noted, while established companies have less incentive to pay for the newest models if cheaper alternatives can do the job.

That creates a problem for AI providers hoping to turn growing adoption into a lasting revenue stream. Selling more computing power and model access can boost suppliers’ sales, but customers need to see corresponding gains in productivity, revenue or operating costs to keep spending at the same pace. Moreover, if AI expenses rise without a measurable improvement in business performance, the additional spending could weigh on margins.

“AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.” Slok added. “The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector.”

Slok’s analysis also points to a broader limitation: AI adoption remains concentrated among a relatively small group of companies. Unless usage spreads across more industries and produces measurable results, the technology’s effect on the wider economy could remain limited.

The same tension is emerging in India’s financial technology sector. A PwC India survey reported by Business Standard on September 11 found that 84% of surveyed fintech respondents had yet to see measurable financial results from their AI investments.

That has not stopped companies from pressing ahead. The survey also found that 48% of respondents identified proprietary intelligence as a leading strategic priority. Meanwhile, 30% expected customer experience to drive AI agent adoption over the next three to five years, followed by cost reduction and productivity gains at 22%.

Trust is another hurdle for businesses looking to deploy AI agents in financial services . As per the survey, 41% of respondents identified customer trust and adoption as the biggest barriers to scaling agentic payments, while 33% pointed to fraud, security and risk management as major concerns.

AI agents could expand the technology’s role in business by handling multistep tasks rather than simply responding to prompts, although their ability to access tools, process information and act across company systems also brings additional usage costs and security concerns.

Nvidia has been developing tools to address some of those risks, previously, introducing its Open Agent Safety Platform , a hardware-and-software security stack designed to help businesses control AI agents and restrict potentially harmful actions. Rising token consumption has also prompted companies including Microsoft , Meta and Amazon to rein in AI usage as employees adopt the tools and agentic workloads drive up bills. The trend highlights a growing challenge for businesses: encouraging wider AI adoption without allowing operating costs to spiral.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has also acknowledged the problem, describing AI token costs as a “huge issue” for customers seeking better value from their spending. The infrastructure behind the AI boom carries its own price tag with Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft having committed enormous sums to data centers, chips and the power needed to run AI workloads.

Corporate America is starting to see AI spending not as a source of growth, but as a cost center. One of the world's largest investment firms says that only tech companies are getting a share of the AI pie . In an economic analysis published on Saturday, Apollo Global Management said that while the Magnificent Seven — a group of established tech companies that includes Nvidia and Meta — are seeing revenue growth during the AI boom, this growth isn't being shared by other industries. "Mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Torsten Slok, a partner and chief economist at Apollo, said in the report. "The technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech." In a series of graphs, Slok measured three main metrics that have boomed for tech companies but not for regular companies: revenue per worker, profit margins, and productivity growth. Since 2022, revenue per employee figures have skyrocketed for tech companies — rising from $550,000 to nearly $800,000 today. Meanwhile, that figure hasn't changed much for everyone else in the S&P 500, lingering around $550,000 for the last seven years. Similarly, while profit margins soared among tech companies since 2022, they've stagnated at about 10% for everyone else. And across the economy, AI hasn't yet dramatically increased productivity growth as some AI optimists have predicted. Apollo's research portends a dark shadow over a US economy throwing massive amounts of dough toward AI tools and companies, whose leaders have promised that an " age of abundance ," where people won't have to work as much, will soon be upon us. "The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins," Slok said. "That may be harder than it sounds," he added. If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

Torsten Slok's October 24 note found flat margins and revenue per worker across the S&P 493, even as Microsoft guides to $190 billion in 2026 AI capex and Meta plans up to $135 billion. Seven companies are carrying an AI boom that, by one economist's math, has yet to show up anywhere else in corporate America. That gap is now the central argument of the AI bubble skeptics. Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, published a note on October 24 making a specific, checkable claim: revenue per worker and profit margins have climbed for the Magnificent Seven since the AI spending wave began, and have stayed essentially flat for the other 493 companies in the S&P 500. Slok's own phrase for it, reported by Bloomberg, was that AI has delivered "zero payoff" to that broader group. Companies outside the Mag 7 are mentioning AI constantly on earnings calls, he found, but the mentions aren't translating into the numbers that are supposed to follow: faster revenue growth, fatter margins, or real cost savings. Slok's framing, also picked up by Fortune, is that mainstream corporate America is starting to treat AI token spending less like an investment and more like a cost center weighing on margins. That's a blunt reversal of the pitch every enterprise AI vendor has been selling for two years. If the companies buying the tools can't point to the return, the sales pitch has a hole in it.
